An application for registration must specify the name and address of the applicant, along with a statement confirming that the layout-design has not been previously registered or published anywhere. The Controller General may require such further information as is necessary to ascertain compliance with these provisions; provided that any prior publication by a government authority acting in its sovereign capacity shall be disregarded for the purpose of determining eligibility for registration. Failure to comply with prescribed forms and procedures will render an application liable to rejection.

For the purposes of this Act, "registered proprietor" includes any person who is recorded as the owner of a trademark in the Register; and “registered user” shall mean a person to whom a license has been granted by the registered proprietor for use of the trademark. A registered user shall be entitled to institute proceedings concerning infringement of the trade mark subject to the terms of the licence agreement, provided that such agreement is filed with the Trademarks Registry. The rights conferred upon a registered user are not absolute and may be limited by express provisions within the license or by subsequent amendments made to the Register reflecting changes in ownership or permitted use. Any assignment of a trademark shall not affect existing rights of a registered user unless expressly agreed to in writing.

For the purposes of this Act, a "registered user" shall be deemed to possess for all intents and purposes the title to the trademark as if directly registered. Any proprietor may grant registration privileges relating to specific geographical territories or product classes within their exclusive rights; such grants shall create a legally recognized “registered user” with standing to pursue remedies for infringement identical to those afforded the original proprietor, subject to any limitations expressly defined in the assignment agreement. The proprietor retains ultimate control over quality assurance and brand standards applicable to goods bearing the trademark used by a registered user. A registered user’s rights are not transferable without prior written consent from the proprietor, provided that such consent shall not be unreasonably withheld.

For the purposes of this Act, "registered user" with respect to a trademark shall mean any person prescribed under rules made by the Trade Marks Registry and who has been duly authorized by the proprietor of the trade mark to use such trade mark. Such authorization may be granted subject to conditions as the Registrar deems fit, which conditions shall be recorded in the Register of Registered Users. A registered user shall possess the right to institute proceedings concerning infringement of the trademark on behalf of the proprietor, provided that such proceedings are conducted consistent with the terms and limitations prescribed within the authorizing agreement. The rights conferred upon a registered user shall not extend beyond the scope of goods or services for which registration has been granted.

For the purposes of this Act, "registered user" with respect to a trademark shall mean any person who has been duly authorized by the proprietor of the trademark to use such trademark under a license agreement and whose name is entered into the Register of Trade Marks as such. A registered user shall be entitled to institute proceedings concerning the remedies available under this Act in the same manner as if he were the proprietor, subject to the terms of his registration. The particulars of any registered user, including the extent of their authorized use, shall be published in the Official Gazette for public information. Any alteration or revocation of a registered user’s authorization must also be notified through publication in the Official Gazette.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to include a statement indicating intention to use the mark in relation to goods or services specified in the application. Where the applicant is a company which is not yet incorporated at the time of filing, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish an affidavit verifying that the incorporation process is underway and specifying a reasonable timeframe for completion. Failure to provide such an affidavit within the period stipulated by the Registrar shall render the application liable to be refused. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the Registrar regarding the acceptance or rejection of an application based on intended use may appeal to the High Court, subject to payment of prescribed fees.

Any proprietor of a registered trade mark who alleges that any other person is using a trade mark which is identical or confusingly similar to his own, and without due cause, shall be entitled to institute proceedings in the High Court for an injunction restraining the use of the infringing mark. The plaintiff may also claim damages sustained by him as a consequence of the infringement, subject to proof of such loss. Provided that where the defendant proves having used the impugned trade mark prior to the date of registration of the plaintif’s trade mark, and without intent to deceive or cause confusion, the Court may grant leave permitting continued use for a limited period, determined at its discretion, upon such terms as it deems just.

For the purposes of this Act, “territory” means India and includes any territory outside India where the Trade Marks Registry has been authorized to grant registration; "trade mark" with its grammatical inflections and cognates means a mark capable of distinguishing goods offered for sale in one enterprise from those of others and may include a coloured or three-dimensional shape which is not merely descriptive, provided that such shape does not comply with any statutory requirement. An application for the registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be made in respect of all classes of goods or services specified in Schedule I unless the applicant specifies fewer classes; however, an applicant may request the High Court to determine whether a particular good or service falls within a class.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if the proposed marks include any representation which, by its nature, is capable of distinguishing goods or services of one undertaking from those of another but contains matter that is descriptive of the characteristics of the goods or services and has been used in relation to such goods or services prior to the date of application. Where an applicant intends to use a trade mark for a company yet to be incorporated, they shall furnish evidence satisfactory to the Registrar confirming their intention; failure to do so may result in removal from the register. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the Registrar regarding inclusion on the register may appeal to the High Court within sixty days.

An application for registration of a trade mark may be assigned by the applicant to any person or entity with their consent, provided that the assignor’s interest in the application is clearly defined within the instrument of assignment. Such an instrument must be executed as a deed, unless it takes effect under seal; and shall contain a verification by the assignee confirming acceptance of the trade mark rights upon registration. The Trade Marks Registry may require production of such verification at any time during the pendency of the application or subsequent to registration. Failure to provide this verification within thirty days of request will render the assignment voidable at the Registrar’s discretion, subject to due process and opportunity for explanation being afforded to all parties concerned.

An assignment of a trade mark, whether absolute or partial, shall be effected by instrument in writing. Such instrument must clearly identify both the assignor and assignee by their registered names as appearing on the Register of Trade Marks; provided that where the assignee is not already recorded upon the Register, the application for registration thereof accompanies the assignment. The assignment shall also specify with particularity the goods or services to which the trade mark relates. Where an assignment involves a partial transfer of rights, the instrument must delineate precisely those rights transferred and those retained by the assignor. Any assignment executed outside India requires notarization and attestation in accordance with regulations prescribed by the Trade Marks Registry.

An application for registration of a trade mark may be made by or on behalf of any person claiming to be the proprietor of the trade mark, but where the right to the trade mark is derived through *assignment*, such application shall state the full details of the assignment, including the date thereof and the consideration given. The Central Government may require evidence satisfactory to it that the applicant is entitled to make the application by virtue of the said assignment. Where an assignment relates only to part of a trade mark, the application must clearly define the portion assigned. Further, any subsequent *assignment* shall be recorded in the Register of Trade Marks and shall take effect from the date on which such recordal is effected, subject to prior rights.

An application for registration of a trade mark may be assigned by the applicant to any person who is not already registered proprietor of that trade mark, provided that the assignor provides written notice of the assignment to the Registrar within three months of its execution. Such notice shall include details sufficient to identify both the assigning and receiving parties, as well as a clear description of the trade mark being assigned. Failure to provide such notification will render the assignee not a party to the application until registration is complete. The right to file any subsequent document relating to the application, including but not limited to requests for amendment or statements of use, shall vest solely in the registered proprietor following completion of the assignment.

For the purposes of this Act, a “breeder” shall be deemed to include any person who has exercised skill and care in selecting, crossing, hybridizing, mutating, or otherwise breeding plants for the purpose of developing new plant varieties. The Authority may, upon receiving an application from any individual claiming to be a breeder, conduct such inquiries as it deems necessary to ascertain whether the applicant fulfills the criteria outlined herein. Such inquiries shall include verification of records pertaining to lineage and propagation techniques employed. An applicant failing to provide satisfactory documentation or demonstrating insufficient skill in plant breeding practices may have their claim rejected by the Authority after due opportunity for representation has been afforded. The decision of the Authority is final, subject to appeal before a designated appellate forum.

For the purposes of this Act, a “breeder” shall be deemed to have fulfilled their obligations regarding farmers’ rights if they provide, free of charge for at least three successive generations, sufficient quantities of basic planting material derived from a protected variety to progressive growers in regions designated by the Authority as areas experiencing hardship due to drought or flood. This provision is subject to verification through reports submitted annually by registered seed distributors and confirmed by inspection teams dispatched by the Authority. Provided that, if a breeder demonstrates compliance with established protocols for conservation of genetic resources relating to the same protected variety, they may petition the Authority for an exemption from this requirement concerning basic planting material distribution; such petitions shall be considered based on scientific merit and regional need assessments conducted by the Authority.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person claiming to be a *breeder* shall make an *application* in the prescribed form to the Authority for registration of a plant variety. Such application shall include particulars relating to the origin of the variety, its method of breeding, genetic composition, stability over successive generations, and such other information as may be required by the Authority. The Authority may reject any application if it determines that the claimed novelty is not established or if the applicant has failed to disclose material facts relevant to the assessment of the plant variety’s distinctiveness. An aggrieved applicant may appeal against an order of rejection to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of such order.

For the purposes of this Act, a “breeder” shall be deemed to include any person who has exercised skill and ingenuity in developing a new plant variety. Such determination is subject to verification by the Authority regarding compliance with established documentation protocols pertaining to lineage tracing and phenotypic expression. A breeder seeking registration of a novel plant variety must provide detailed records demonstrating adherence to prescribed isolation distances during propagation, ensuring genetic purity consistent with accepted industry standards. The Authority may require further evidence substantiating claims of novelty if prior public disclosure is suspected. Furthermore, the breeder shall attest that all parentage material utilized in development was obtained legally and without infringing upon existing plant variety rights.

Where an application for registration is opposed under this Act, and such opposition is ultimately resolved in favour of the applicant, the Registrar shall record the particulars of the opposition and its resolution in the Register of Trade Marks. Any subsequent dealings with the trade mark, including but not limited to assignments, licenses, or changes in name of the registered proprietor, shall be subject to scrutiny by the Registrar to ensure compliance with the terms of the resolved opposition. The registered proprietor shall provide all documentation requested by the Registrar pertaining to such prior proceedings and any subsequent alterations affecting rights derived therefrom. Failure to comply may result in a refusal to register the dealing or amendment.

Subject to any direction made under this Act, where an application for registration is refused, the applicant may appeal against such refusal within three months from the date of communication of the refusal. The Appellate Board shall hear and determine the appeal expeditiously; provided that the appellant must demonstrate demonstrable prejudice arising directly from the refusal. Further, in instances involving a challenge to the validity of a registered trade mark based on use predating registration, the burden of proof regarding prior honest usage rests upon the challenger. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may petition the Supreme Court within sixty days; however, the *registered proprietor* retains all rights and remedies pending such determination.

For the purposes of this Act, where an application for registration is opposed under sub-rule (1) of rule 35 and the Registrar determines that the opposition is frivolous or vexatious, he may direct the opponent to pay costs to the applicant. Such direction shall specify the amount of costs payable, which may include reasonable expenses incurred by the applicant in connection with the proceedings before the Registrar. The registered proprietor shall be entitled to receive such sum as directed. Further, any appeal against an order made under this provision is subject to a stay application being filed within thirty days of the order’s communication and accompanied by payment of prescribed fees. Failure to comply renders the appeal inadmissible.

Where an application for registration is made in respect of a composite mark comprising words, devices or three-dimensional features, and such mark includes references to geographical indications as defined under another Act, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating that the use of said geographical indication does not constitute misleading representation concerning the origin of goods. Further, if the application relates to an associated trade mark, registration shall be conditional upon a declaration by the registered proprietor confirming ongoing compliance with any terms or conditions stipulated in the original trade mark’s registration certificate and acknowledging liability for infringement arising from unauthorized use thereof. The registered proprietor shall also provide undertakings as deemed necessary by the Controller regarding continued adherence to quality standards.

For the purposes of this Act, “author” with respect to a musical work shall include not only the composer but also the lyricist where words are set to music. Where such composition is created jointly by two or more individuals, each individual shall be deemed an *author* for the portion of the work they contributed. The contribution may consist of either the musical elements, the lyrical content, or a combination thereof. For works produced under arrangements made by employers, the author shall be determined as follows: if the work is substantially attributable to one person’s effort and skill, that person shall be considered the *author*; otherwise, both the employee and the employer may jointly claim authorship, subject to such terms of assignment as are explicitly agreed upon in writing.

For the purposes of this Act, where a work is created jointly by authors residing in different countries, and registration for copyright is sought, the applicant shall declare the nationality of each contributing author. Where an author’s place of residence has been continuously altered over a substantial period during the creation of the work, and establishing definitive nationality proves challenging, the Copyright Board may, upon review of submitted documentation including affidavits from the applicant and any dissenting authors, determine for administrative purposes which nation shall be considered the primary jurisdiction for copyright registration. This determination shall not prejudice claims regarding infringement or enforcement actions undertaken elsewhere. The Registrar may require further evidence to substantiate claimed authorship in such cases.

For the purposes of this Act, where a cinematograph film incorporates elements created by multiple individuals, and establishing definitive authorship proves challenging due to collaborative contributions, the individual who exercises primary creative control over the arrangement and selection of such elements shall be deemed the *author* for determining copyright ownership. Provided that, if no single individual demonstrably fulfils this criterion, joint authorship may be attributed; in which case, rights pertaining to the work are held concurrently by all jointly recognized authors. Any subsequent grant of a licence concerning the film’s use or reproduction must explicitly identify and acknowledge all contributing authors as per their respective contributions documented within production records maintained by the copyright holder.

For the purposes of this Act, “author” with respect to a computer program shall include the person who causes the program to be created. Where such creation extends over a considerable period and involves contributions from multiple individuals, the determination of authorship shall consider the extent of each individual’s contribution towards the final form of the work. The copyright in any such program shall vest initially in the entity employing or contracting with those contributing to its development, provided that such employment or contract explicitly assigns ownership to said entity. Notice of assignment shall be published in the Official Gazette for a period not less than three months from the date of assignment. Any subsequent transfer of this copyright must also be similarly notified.

For the purposes of this Act, an application for registration of a proposed trademark shall be refused if it is deemed identical or confusingly similar to a previously registered trademark. This determination shall consider not only the visual appearance and phonetic similarity of the marks but also their respective goods or services. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit evidence demonstrating that there exists no likelihood of confusion among consumers, should such a claim be raised by an existing proprietor of a registered trade mark. Further, any use of a trademark which creates a false or misleading impression about the nature, quality, or origin of goods or services shall constitute infringement and render the user liable for damages to the owner of the registered trade mark.

Subject to any direction from the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, where an owner of a registered trade mark institutes proceedings for infringement, and it is established that the defendant has made sales infringing upon the said registered trade mark, the Court may grant such remedy as it deems just and equitable. This includes, but is not limited to, an injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of infringement, the delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark, and compensation for damages sustained by the owner. The amount of compensation shall be determined having regard to the loss suffered by the plaintiff, the profit made by the defendant, and any other relevant factors deemed appropriate by the Court. Further, costs incidental to such proceedings may also be awarded.

For the purposes of this Act, an application for registration of a proposed registered trade mark shall be deemed refused if the marks applied for, or any combination thereof, are identical or confusingly similar to a previously registered trade mark used in connection with identical or closely related goods or services. Where such refusal is based on similarity to an earlier registered trade mark, the applicant may submit counter-arguments demonstrating distinctiveness acquired through use subsequent to the date of that prior registration. The Registrar shall consider any evidence presented by the applicant and may request further information from the proprietor of the existing registered trade mark concerning its usage and reputation in relation to the goods or services specified therein.

Any proprietor of a registered trade mark aggrieved by any act of another which constitutes an infringement of his rights under this Act may institute suit for damages sustained thereby. Such damages shall be assessed, subject to proof of proximate causation between the infringing activity and the diminution of sales or goodwill attributable to the plaintiff’s goods or services. Further, where notice of such infringement is published in the Official Gazette by the Registrar at the request of the proprietor, any subsequent act of infringement occurring after the date of publication shall be presumed to have been committed with knowledge of the infringement unless the defendant proves otherwise. The Court may also grant an injunction restraining further acts of infringement and order delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark.

Where a plant variety protection holder unreasonably withholds authorization for conducting research relating to the registered traits of the protected variety, thereby hindering advancements beneficial to agricultural practices, the Authority may, subject to due process and after providing an opportunity for objection by the concerned protection holder, make an order granting a compulsory licence. Such license shall permit any person to perform acts which would otherwise constitute infringement of the plant breeder’s rights, but only to the extent necessary for conducting the research as specified in the order. The terms and conditions of such compulsory licence, including royalty payments proportionate to the use made, shall be determined by the Authority.

The Authority may, upon application made by any person demonstrating a compelling need for access to a protected plant variety, grant a compulsory licence. Such an application shall include detailed particulars regarding the nature of the need, the extent of cultivation proposed, and safeguards against unauthorized propagation. The applicant must further demonstrate that reasonable efforts have been undertaken to obtain authorization from the right holder on mutually acceptable terms. Prior to issuing any order for a compulsory licence, the Authority shall provide notice to the plant breeder entitled to protection and offer an opportunity for them to be heard. Any fee determined by the Authority shall be payable by the applicant as a condition precedent to exercising rights granted under the compulsory licence.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall be deemed to have been made in bad faith if the applicant has demonstrably misrepresented data pertaining to its expression stability during field trials. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint from any person demonstrating that such misrepresentation has substantially prejudiced access to essential germplasm or hindered agricultural innovation, initiate an inquiry. If, following such inquiry, it is determined that the plant variety registration was obtained through fraudulent means, the Authority shall have power to make an order for a compulsory licence, permitting other persons to produce and utilize the registered variety subject to equitable terms and conditions as may be prescribed.

Where a plant variety protection grant holder fails demonstrably to meet reasonable demands for seed quantities sufficient to ensure adequate propagation by farmers within the territory of India, the Authority may, following due inquiry and after giving notice to the grant holder and an opportunity to be heard, make an order granting a compulsory licence. Such order shall specify the terms and conditions under which the license is granted, including royalty rates not exceeding three percent of the aggregate sales of the harvested produce derived from the protected variety. The Authority shall publish notification of any such compulsory licence in the Official Gazette. Any aggrieved party may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of publication in the Official Gazette.

For the purposes of this Act, “sound recording” means a recording of sounds fixed permanently on any medium which can be reproduced. Where a sound recording incorporates elements constituting an artistic work, copyright therein shall subsist independently in such artistic element subject to the rights of the owner of the copyright in the sound recording itself. Any person desiring to make use of a sound recording for commercial purposes other than private or domestic use shall apply to the Controller for permission. The application shall specify the nature and extent of the proposed use, along with details regarding remuneration offered to the right holder. The Controller may grant such permission upon receiving written consent from the owner of the copyright in the sound recording, accompanied by a mutually agreed-upon royalty schedule.

For the purposes of this Act, a sound recording shall be deemed copyrightable subject matter provided that such recording originates from India or is commercially distributed within Indian territory. The right subsists only where the producer of the sound recording has exercised sufficient control over its creation and subsequent reproduction. Any alteration to a sound recording which results in a substantial change to the original artistic expression, as determined by an adjudicating authority, shall be considered a new work requiring separate copyright registration. Furthermore, any use of a protected sound recording for broadcasting purposes requires prior written consent from the producer unless such usage falls within the parameters defined under fair dealing provisions relating to journalistic reporting or educational instruction.

For the purposes of this Act, infringement of copyright in a sound recording shall include any unauthorized reproduction, distribution, public exhibition, or adaptation thereof. Where such infringement involves the use of a trade mark associated with the original sound recording to falsely suggest endorsement or affiliation by the owner of that trade mark, the remedies available under this Act may be augmented by claims for damages relating to dilution and unfair competition. Any person found to have infringed copyright in a sound recording shall be liable to pay such compensation as the Court deems fit, taking into account the extent of the infringement and any resulting loss suffered by the owner of the copyright. The right to seek injunctions restraining further acts of infringement is expressly preserved.

For the purposes of this Act, a “sound recording” shall be deemed an artistic work and copyright therein shall subsist until sixty years from the end of the year in which the sound recording is first published. Any person who reproduces, distributes, performs publicly, broadcasts, or communicates to the public any substantial portion of a protected sound recording without due authorization from the owner of the copyright shall be guilty of infringement. The Tribunal may, upon receiving complaint regarding such alleged infringement, issue interim orders restraining further acts of reproduction or distribution pending final determination. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this provision may appeal to the High Court within sixty days of the date of such order.

Applications for registration of a trade mark shall be filed at such office of the Trade Marks Registry as the Registrar may direct. The Registrar may, from time to time, establish additional offices of the Trade Marks Registry, specifying their territorial jurisdiction in a notification published in the Official Gazette. Any person seeking to obtain information regarding the status of an application or registered trade mark must submit a written request to the relevant office; such requests shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee. The Registrar may require applicants and proprietors to conduct all correspondence through designated postal channels, as specified on the Trade Marks Registry website. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements may result in delays or rejection of submissions, subject to appeal before an Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

For the purpose of this Act, “official record” means any document maintained by the Trade Marks Registry relating to applications for registration, registrations, oppositions, rectifications, caveats, licenses, assignments, renewals, and other proceedings before the Registry; such records shall be deemed conclusive evidence of matters therein recorded, subject to proof of due execution or proper attestation. “Hearing” includes a hearing conducted in person, electronically, or through video conferencing as may be prescribed by the Trade Marks Registry. The term "applicant" shall include any individual, partnership, company, or association applying for registration under this Act and shall extend to their authorized agents. Any reference to the Trade Marks Registry shall be construed as including references to all offices of the Trade Marks Registry functioning throughout India.

The Director shall maintain a register of applications for registration of trade marks, which register shall be open to public inspection during normal office hours. Any person may inspect such register and obtain certified copies thereof upon payment of prescribed fees. The Trade Marks Registry may, at its discretion, publish extracts from the register in any manner it deems appropriate, including electronic dissemination. Applications received by the Trade Marks Registry shall be examined for compliance with this Act and the Regulations made thereunder. Objections to an application may be raised by any interested party within the time specified; such objections shall be considered by the Registrar who shall provide a reasoned order regarding their admissibility. The register shall accurately reflect the status of each trade mark application or registration.

Applications for registration of a trade mark shall be filed at such office of the Trade Marks Registry as the Registrar may direct. The Registrar may, generally or in any particular case, specify the form of applications and statements of particulars required under this Act. Any applicant desiring to file an application relating to goods or services classified within different classes shall submit separate applications for each class, accompanied by the requisite fees. Where an application is found to be deficient in compliance with prescribed forms or contains material misstatements, the Registrar may require the applicant to rectify such deficiencies or withdraw the application entirely. The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a record of all filed and examined trade marks accessible to the public upon payment of applicable charges.

For the purposes of this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,—(a) "guarantee" with reference to a certification trade mark shall mean a guarantee that the goods or services in relation to which the certification trade mark is used satisfy particular requirements; (b) “certification trade mark owner” means an organisation recognised by the Registrar as being suitable to administer and control a certification trade mark, subject to such conditions of recognition as may be prescribed; (c) "certified person" means a person who has been certified by the certification trade mark owner as having satisfied the requirements for goods or services eligible for certification; (d) “certification standard” means the standards established by the certification trade mark owner which must be met before goods or services can be certified. The Registrar may, at any time, require the certification trade mark owner to furnish information relating to its activities and compliance with this Act.

For the purposes of registration, a certification trade mark shall be distinctive in its character and indicate that the certified products or services conform to a defined standard, specification, characteristic, quality, origin, production method, or other attribute as determined by an authority constituted for that purpose. The applicant for registration of a certification trade mark must demonstrate that it is authorized to use such mark by the said authority and shall provide evidence of the constitution, powers, and functions of that authority. Use of the certification trade mark shall be restricted to persons who comply with the standards established by the controlling authority; provided that nothing in this provision prevents the use of the mark by the authority itself or its agents.

For the purposes of this Act, a certification trade mark shall be defined as a mark that identifies agricultural products, foodstuffs, textiles, handicrafts, or other goods meeting specified standards relating to origin, process, quality, materials, fitness for purpose, or characteristics. An application for registration as a certification trade mark must demonstrate adherence to established protocols and procedures approved by the Registrar. The applicant shall provide detailed specifications outlining the conditions under which goods bearing the certification trade mark may be certified; provided that such conditions are verifiable and non-discriminatory. Any alteration of these specified standards requires prior notification and approval from the relevant regulatory body, ensuring continued compliance with prescribed guidelines.

For the purposes of registration, a certification trade mark shall be distinctive if it signifies that the certified products or services conform to certain specified standards, characteristics, qualities, or production methods established by the applicant. The applicant must demonstrate control over the use of the certification trade mark and ensure adherence to the defined criteria. Such standards may relate to geographical origin, manufacturing processes, or other relevant attributes. Nothing in this Act shall prevent registration if the proposed mark is descriptive of a patented invention relating to the certified product’s composition or method of manufacture, provided that such description does not directly indicate the patent holder's identity and use is authorized by them. The Registrar may require evidence substantiating these standards and control mechanisms during examination.

For the purposes of this Act, an application for registration as a *performer* shall be accompanied by a certified copy of any contract entered into between the performer and the producer of the cinematograph film, detailing the scope of performance and remuneration agreed upon. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the nature and extent of the performer’s contribution to the work. Where a collective bargaining agreement governs the terms of engagement for a *performer*, such agreement shall be deemed sufficient evidence of contractual obligations subject to verification by the Registrar. Any alteration or addition to the original performance, not explicitly consented to in writing by the registered *performer*, constitutes an infringement of their rights under this Act and renders the derivative work liable for action.

For the purposes of this Act, a *performer* shall be deemed to include any person who delivers a performance before an audience. Any such performer shall have the right to prevent, subject to reasonable use for criticism or review, the reproduction in any form of substantial portions of their performance without their authorization. Where such authorization is not granted, any unauthorized reproduction constitutes infringement and renders the infringer liable to damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the performer, but not exceeding an amount as may be determined by a competent court. Provided that this right shall not extend to performances broadcast or communicated to the public under license from appropriate authorities.

For the purposes of this Act, "performer" includes an actor, dancer, musician, and singer. A performer shall be deemed to have performed any work in relation to which he has exercised skill and judgment in its presentation or reproduction. Where a performance is fixed on phonograms, the performer’s right subsists irrespective of whether such fixation was prescribed by contract or otherwise. The term "performer" extends to individuals contributing significantly to the creation of an artistic rendition through their actions, subject to the condition that such contribution constitutes a substantial and identifiable element within the final work. Any alteration or adaptation affecting the integrity of a performer’s performance shall be prohibited without express authorization.

For the purposes of this Act, registration of a *performer’s* right shall be deemed conclusive evidence of ownership, subject to demonstrable proof of fraudulent intent at the time of application. An applicant seeking such registration must submit detailed documentation pertaining to the performance itself, including dates, venues, and any incorporated design elements utilized in stagecraft or costume. The Registrar may require further affidavits from collaborating artists or production personnel confirming the performer’s substantial contribution. Where a *performer* incorporates pre-existing copyrighted material into their act, such as musical compositions or literary excerpts, explicit written consent from the copyright holder shall be appended to the registration application. Failure to provide this documentation may result in rejection of the application.

The Registrar may, upon application by a proprietor of a registered trade mark, enter alterations to particulars relating to ownership where such alteration is evidenced by a formal instrument executed in accordance with prescribed procedures. Any modification concerning the geographical extent of protection afforded by a registered trade mark shall be accompanied by proof satisfactory to the Registrar that consumer recognition and association with the applicant’s goods or services are demonstrably limited to the specified territory. Further, any representation on the register indicating a change in class of goods or services for which registration is sought must comply with established classification guidelines and not create confusion likely to mislead consumers regarding the origin of those goods or services relative to existing registered trade marks.

The Registrar may, upon application by any person claiming ownership or a substantial interest in copyright relating to literary works used as part of a registered trade mark, direct that an entry be made on the Register indicating the existence of such copyright. Such entry shall serve as notice to third parties regarding potential limitations on use and reproduction of the copyrighted material consistent with the rights afforded to the proprietor of the registered trade marks. Any alteration or addition to the Register concerning copyright information must be authenticated by the official seal of the Trade Marks Registry, and a certified copy thereof may be admissible in evidence. The Registrar shall maintain records pertaining to these entries for a period not less than ten years from the date of such entry.

The Registrar may, upon application by the registered proprietor of a trademark, direct that any other trademark previously registered be deemed to be an associated trademark for the purposes of this Act. Such direction shall specify the relationship between the trademarks and apply only to goods or services identical or closely related to those in respect of which both trademarks are registered. The applicant shall provide evidence demonstrating consumer recognition of such association. Any party aggrieved by a decision under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. This process does not affect any rights or remedies available against *trade marks registered* prior to the operative date of this direction.

For the purposes of this Act, a “composite mark” is defined as a trade mark consisting of words, devices, or other indications arranged in such a manner that they convey a composite impression distinct from the impressions created by the individual elements considered separately. Where a composite mark includes any element identical or similar to previously registered trademarks, registration shall be refused if use thereof would create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods or services. The Registrar may allow registration of a composite mark subject to limitations restricting its use to specific goods or services and requiring prominent display of all constituent elements. Any application for registration of a trade marks registered as associated trade marks must clearly identify the relationship between the applied-for mark and the existing trademark.

The Registrar may, upon application by the registered proprietor of a trademark, direct that any patent granted subsequent to the date of first use of the said trademark shall be deemed to incorporate an acknowledgement of the prior existence and continuing validity of the trade marks registered. Such direction shall specify the manner in which this acknowledgement is to appear on all documents relating to the patent, including but not limited to published specifications and renewal notices. The application for such a direction must include evidence demonstrating that the patented invention utilizes or relates directly to goods or services identifiable with the trademark. Failure to comply with procedural requirements outlined in Form TM-P7 shall render the application void ab initio.

For the purposes of determining novelty under this Act, prior use or knowledge of an invention shall not constitute anticipation unless it is documented in tangible form accessible to the public. An application for a patent may be made by any person claiming to be the inventor, or by any party authorized to make such an application on behalf of the applicant; provided that where a person has derived title to the invention from the true and first inventor, they shall disclose particulars of the derivation in their application. The Controller General may require applicants seeking patents for processes relating to substances produced by fermentation to submit detailed specifications outlining the microbial strains employed and conditions maintained during production. Any alteration made to an applied process after filing must be reported within three months.

The Registering Authority shall prescribe the form and manner of application for registration of a patent. Every applicant shall furnish with their application particulars relating to priority, if any claim is made on the basis thereof; failing which, the application may be rejected. The Central Government may require such fees as it deems fit to be paid in respect of applications for patents and for subsequent proceedings related to registration. An applicant who has previously filed an identical patent application in a country outside India shall disclose this fact in their application, along with details pertaining to the date of filing and status of that prior registration. The Registering Authority may request further documentation or clarification from applicants during the examination process to ensure completeness of the patent registration record.

For the purposes of this Act, “farmer” includes both individual agricultural practitioners and groups of individuals engaged in collective farming activities. A farmer shall be deemed to possess rights over plant varieties cultivated by them for propagation or sale, subject to compliance with conditions prescribed under this legislation concerning traceability and benefit sharing. "Community Varieties" means plant varieties evolved, multiplied and disseminated amongst traditional farming communities, and a “farmer” cultivating such Community Varieties is entitled to protection against infringement of their rights in relation to the commercial exploitation of those varieties. The term "farmer" excludes individuals or entities engaged primarily in research or industrial production unrelated to agricultural practices.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a farmer shall be entitled to save, exchange, share or sell farm saved seed of any variety which they have legally obtained. No right granted by this Act shall restrict such entitlement, provided that the farmer does not market the seed under a trademark or plant breeder’s rights denomination without appropriate authorization. Any person who obstructs or prevents a farmer from exercising these rights may be liable to pay compensation as determined by the Authority. The Authority may issue directions for redressal of grievances relating to infringement of farmers' rights, and any order made by the Authority shall be binding on all parties concerned.

For the purposes of this Act, a “farmer” includes any individual cultivating land for agricultural purposes, irrespective of the scale or nature of such cultivation, and who is engaged in propagation, multiplication, exchange, sale, distribution, or conservation of plant material. A farmer shall be deemed to possess inherent rights over varieties propagated by them, subject to compliance with prescribed conditions relating to registration. Where a farmer utilizes saved seed for subsequent plantings, they may apply for voluntary registration of the resultant variety, provided that such application discloses the origin and propagation methods employed. The Authority may grant or refuse registration based on criteria outlined in Schedule B, considering factors including novelty and stability of the registered variety.

For the purposes of this Act, “farmer” includes both those cultivating agricultural land for commercial gain and those engaged in traditional farming practices, irrespective of the scale or nature of their holdings. A farmer shall be deemed to possess rights over varieties cultivated by them, subject to compliance with provisions relating to registration and reporting as prescribed. The term "farmer" also encompasses individuals who are members of a farmers’ collective registered under applicable legislation. Any notification issued pertaining to eligibility criteria for claiming benefits under this Act or concerning the procedures for exercising farmer's rights shall be published in the Official Gazette. Such publication shall constitute official notice, binding on all concerned parties.

The applicant seeking registration of a certification trade mark shall furnish detailed particulars regarding the organization proposing to use the mark, including its constitution, governing body, and financial resources. The Registrar may require such further information as is deemed necessary to ascertain the genuineness of the proposed certifying authority’s commitment to maintaining standards for goods or services certified under the mark. Any alteration in the composition of the certifying body shall be reported to the Registrar within thirty days; failure to do so may render the registration liable for review. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all certification trade marks and details pertaining thereto, accessible for public inspection.

Any applicant seeking application registration for a novel plant variety shall furnish with their initial submission a comprehensive declaration detailing all prior public disclosures pertaining to said variety’s genetic composition and propagation techniques. Failure to provide this declaration constitutes grounds for rejection of the application registration. Where such an omission is discovered post-registration, the Registrar may direct the registrant to rectify the record within ninety days; failing compliance, the plant variety shall be deemed nullified, and any derived commercial benefit attributable to the unregistered status will be subject to recovery as determined by the Authority. The burden of proving due diligence in disclosing prior knowledge rests solely upon the applicant.

An applicant seeking registration of a plant variety shall furnish with the application a detailed description conforming to Form A as prescribed by the Governing Body. This description must include particulars regarding the origin and lineage of the variety, including details of parent lines and any hybridization processes undertaken. Furthermore, an affirmation signed by the applicant attesting to the accuracy and completeness of the information provided is required. The Registrar may request supplementary data or clarification concerning any aspect of the application registration if deemed necessary for a thorough assessment. Any alteration to the particulars submitted after initial filing shall be accompanied by a written explanation justifying the modification.

An applicant seeking registration of a plant variety shall furnish with their application a detailed statement outlining all prior uses and derivations from existing varieties, including precise lineage tracing where applicable. Failure to provide this comprehensive account constitutes grounds for rejection of the application registration. Where an applicant has granted a licence relating to the registered variety before the grant of registration, they must declare the terms of such licences, specifying any restrictions on subsequent generations or geographical limitations. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding these licensing arrangements and reserves the right to refuse registration if the declared terms are deemed unduly restrictive or contrary to public interest in promoting farmer’s rights.

An applicant submitting an application registration for a plant variety shall furnish detailed particulars regarding the method of propagation employed and the stability of characteristics across successive generations. Such particulars must include data from at least three distinct growing seasons conducted in geographically diverse locations representative of intended cultivation areas. The application shall also specify any traits exhibiting segregation or variation, accompanied by quantitative assessments demonstrating conformity to established standards for uniformity. Failure to provide complete and accurate information as stipulated may result in the rejection of the application registration. Any unauthorized use of a registered variety without due authorization constitutes infringement under this Act.

Where a patentee seeks to enforce rights conferred under this Act against any person, and it is demonstrated to the Controller that such enforcement involves the imposition of restrictive conditions upon trade or industrial practices beyond what is reasonably necessary to protect the patent’s subject matter, the Controller shall issue notice to all interested parties. Such notice shall detail the alleged restrictive conditions and provide a period not less than thirty days for objections to be filed. The patentee shall then have an opportunity to respond in writing to any such objection. Following consideration of these submissions, the Controller may determine that the enforcement is unduly burdensome and direct modification or abrogation of the restrictive conditions to ensure proportionality with the legitimate scope of the patent’s protection.

Any agreement relating to the assignment or licensing of rights pertaining to an invention shall not contain conditions that unduly restrict the exploitation of the patent within India. Provided that such restrictive conditions are determined to have the primary purpose or effect of preventing competition amongst entities engaged in similar technological fields, they shall be deemed invalid and unenforceable. The Controller may issue directions requiring parties to amend agreements containing these provisions to ensure compliance with principles of fair trade practices. Further, any condition limiting the importation of materials necessary for implementing a patented process will be subject to review if it demonstrably impedes access to essential technologies within India.

Where a patentee seeks to enforce their rights under this Act against any person, and such enforcement involves allegations that restrictive conditions were imposed upon the licensee’s use or sale of the patented invention, the aggrieved party shall have recourse to remedies available in civil law. The patentee bears the burden of demonstrating that the alleged restrictive condition does not unduly prejudice the interests of trade or innovation within India. Any application for injunctive relief predicated on a claim of infringement arising from such conditions may be stayed if the applicant fails to provide satisfactory evidence, as determined by the Controller, substantiating the reasonableness and necessity of those limitations.

An international registration designating India shall be examined for compliance with all applicable provisions relating to domestic trademark applications. The application’s priority date shall be deemed the filing date for purposes of assessing relative grounds for refusal, subject to verification that the basic application was filed in conformity with the laws of the designated country. Where an earlier mark exists within India identical or similar to a term included in the international registration and used in relation to goods or services identical or similar to those specified in the international registration, the Registrar may refuse registration unless evidence is provided demonstrating lack of likelihood of confusion. The applicant shall be afforded opportunity for response prior to any final determination.

For the purposes of this Act, “international registration” means an application for the extension of protection of a trade mark registered in one country to two or more other countries, made pursuant to the Protocol relating to Madrid; and such application shall be deemed to be an application for registration in India only to the extent that the designation of India is included therein. An international registration shall have effect subject to any limitations contained within the statement of the grounds for refusal applicable under this Act. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating compliance with Article 3(1) of the Protocol, relating to transliteration where a mark contains elements which are not readily intelligible.

An application for an international registration designating India shall be examined according to the provisions applicable to applications filed directly within India, subject to any modifications prescribed by the Regulations concerning the International Registration of Marks. The Trade Marks Registry shall notify particulars of such applications accepted for publication in the Official Gazette. Any opposition to a mark arising from an international registration must adhere to the timelines specified under the regulations and be accompanied by a certified true copy of the relevant extract from the International Bureau’s database. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements may result in the Registrar declining consideration of the opposition. The Registry shall maintain records pertaining to all international registrations, accessible for public inspection as per established protocols.

An international registration designating India shall be examined for compliance with all applicable provisions relating to national registrations. The application for an international registration shall be refused if it contains any representation which is contrary to law or morality, or if its designation of India conflicts with a pending or registered trade mark already on the register. Where the International Bureau transmits information indicating that the earlier mark has been subject to cancellation in another designated contracting country, the Registrar may require further evidence demonstrating continued validity and distinctiveness before proceeding with registration. The applicant shall provide such documentation within ninety days; failure to do so will result in abandonment of the application.

For the purposes of registration, a person shall be deemed to be acting as a *patent agent* if he holds himself out to the public, either directly or through another individual, as possessing special skill and knowledge relating to patents and offering to perform services concerning the preparation, filing, prosecution, maintenance, and relinquishment of patent applications. Any entity employing such an individual shall also register with the Controller, providing details of all individuals acting on its behalf as *patent agents*. The registration shall be renewed every five years by submitting a prescribed form along with the requisite fee. Failure to do so will result in automatic lapse of the registration and prohibition from representing clients before any patent office authority.

For the purposes of registration, a person shall be deemed to be acting as a *patent agent* if he holds himself out, either directly or indirectly, as possessing special skill and knowledge in relation to inventions and patent law, and habitually performs acts for others relating to the preparation, filing, prosecution, maintenance, and enforcement of applications and patents. Any individual seeking registration as a *patent agent* shall submit Form A along with the prescribed fee, detailing prior qualifications including academic degrees in science or engineering, or equivalent experience deemed satisfactory by the Patents Office. The Registrar may require further documentation verifying professional training undertaken to demonstrate competence in patent drafting and examination procedures before proceeding with assessment for registration.

A person shall be deemed to be acting as a patent agent only if such individual possesses a current certificate of registration issued by the Controller, and has complied with all continuing professional development requirements prescribed under regulations framed pursuant thereto. Any entity employing a registered patent agent shall ensure that said agent’s activities remain strictly within the scope of services permitted for registered agents, namely representation before the Patent Office and preparation of applications for patents or related documents. A patent agent may grant a non-exclusive licence relating to matters falling within their professional practice; however, any such licence must be documented in writing and filed with the Controller if it involves assignment of rights pertaining to an invention subject to pending examination.

For the purposes of this Act, “prescribed fee” shall have the meaning assigned to it by the First Schedule. An applicant for registration as a patent agent shall furnish such documents and particulars as may be prescribed. "Registered Patent Agent" means a person whose name is entered in the Register of Patent Agents maintained under regulation 7; provided that any individual previously registered, but subsequently removed from the register, does not qualify as a Registered Patent Agent. The term “representation” with reference to an invention shall include any depiction or description thereof made for the purpose of securing patent protection. Any person acting as a patent agent without being duly registered shall be deemed guilty of an offence and liable to penalty.

Where a patent is granted for an invention relating to a method of using a substance that has been previously known, the Controller may, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, direct that certain restrictive conditions be imposed on the application and enforcement of the patent. Such directions shall only be issued if it appears that the continued validity of the patent would otherwise create or maintain a monopoly which is contrary to public interest. The Controller shall provide written notice to the applicant and any party claiming an interest in the invention, affording them a reasonable opportunity for representation before issuing such direction. Any condition imposed under these provisions may relate to licensing terms, field of use limitations, or other measures deemed necessary by the Controller.

Where a patentee seeks to enforce their rights under this Act against any person, and it is demonstrated that the enforcement action includes an attempt to impose restrictive conditions upon the use, sale, or manufacture of the patented invention beyond the scope reasonably necessary for protecting the patent’s subject matter, the aggrieved party may petition the Controller. The Controller shall inquire into whether such imposed restrictions unduly restrain trade or competition within India. If it is determined that certain restrictive conditions are demonstrably unreasonable and serve primarily to circumvent the intent of promoting innovation and technological advancement, the Controller may grant relief including but not limited to an injunction preventing further enforcement of those specific limitations and awarding compensation for damages incurred.

Where a patent is granted for an invention relating to a method or process applicable to agriculture or horticulture, certain restrictive conditions shall not be permissible within agreements pertaining to the use or exploitation of such patented methods. These conditions are deemed restrictive if they substantially limit the freedom of farmers to utilize saved seed derived from harvested crops cultivated by means of the patented agricultural or horticultural process. The Controller may, upon receiving a representation alleging the presence of such restrictive conditions, direct that the relevant details be entered into the register and further investigate whether the patent’s validity is affected by this imposition. Provided that any condition reasonably necessary to protect the legitimate interests of the patentee shall not be considered restrictive under these provisions.

Where registration of a biological entity derived from a microorganism is sought under this Act, and such registration involves processes utilizing genetically modified organisms, certain restrictive conditions shall apply to subsequent commercial exploitation. Any agreement relating to the transfer or assignment of rights pertaining to the registered biological entity must explicitly state that no condition imposed restricts research analysis. The Central Government may, in its discretion, require a declaration from the applicant confirming adherence to these stipulations and providing assurances regarding non-discriminatory access for bona fide researchers. Failure to comply with this provision renders the registration liable to revocation by the Controller.

Where an application for a compulsory licence is filed with the Controller, the applicant shall furnish three certified copies of the patent in relation to which the licence is sought. The Controller may require the applicant to submit further documentation demonstrating non-availability of the patented invention within India or inadequate public access thereto. Any interested party may, within sixty days from the date of publication of notice of such application under sub-rule (2) of rule fourteen, file objections with the Controller detailing grounds for opposing the grant of a compulsory licence. The Controller shall afford an opportunity to both the patentee and the applicant to be heard in respect of any objection received. Decisions regarding applications for compulsory licences shall be made within twelve months from the date of their receipt by the Controller.

The Copyright Office shall maintain registers, one each for authors, copyright owners, and works in respect of which copyright has been assigned or relinquished. Applications for registration of literary, dramatic, musical, artistic, and cinematograph film works may be submitted electronically through the designated online portal, accompanied by the prescribed fee. The Registrar of Copyrights may require applicants to furnish such further information as he deems necessary for verification purposes. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Copyright Office relating to the registration or rejection thereof may appeal to an Appellate Board constituted under this Act within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. Records pertaining to copyright ownership and author declarations shall be deemed public documents subject to restrictions imposed in accordance with regulations framed by the Central Government.

Applications for registration of copyright, submitted in accordance with prescribed forms and accompanied by the requisite fee, shall be examined by an officer designated by the Registrar of Copyrights. Any applicant failing to comply with stipulated requirements regarding submission of certified copies of works or providing adequate bibliographic details may have their application deemed incomplete and subject to rejection. The Copyright Office maintains a publicly accessible register detailing all registered copyrights; however, entries are provisional pending verification against existing records and any objections raised within the prescribed timeframe by third parties claiming prior rights. Any alteration or addition to the Register shall be authenticated with the official seal of the Copyright Office and countersigned by the Registrar.

The Copyright Office shall entertain applications from authors seeking to relinquish all or any portion of their copyright in respect of works, provided that such application is made voluntarily and without duress. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the author’s intent and confirming due consideration has been given to the potential impact on derivative works. The Central Government shall be notified of all relinquishments processed by the Copyright Office. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Copyright Office regarding the acceptance or rejection of such an application, or concerning the validity of a relinquished copyright, may appeal to the Controller appointed under this Act within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision.

The Copyright Office shall maintain registers, one each for copyright registrations, renewal applications, and public domain declarations. Applications submitted to the Copyright Office must be accompanied by the prescribed fee and three copies of the work in question or relevant materials. The Registrar may require applicants to furnish further documentation demonstrating ownership or authorship as deemed necessary. Notices regarding accepted registrations, relinquished copyrights, and any amendments thereto shall be published in the Official Gazette for public information. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Copyright Office relating to registration or renewal may appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of such decision; provided that the Registrar’s order shall be binding pending the outcome of said appeal.

For the purposes of this Act, “good” means goods of agricultural origin including foodstuff, livestock, fish, wine and spirits, horticultural products, yarn and handloom fabrics. "Distinctiveness" in relation to a geographical indication registered shall mean that the connection between the good and the territory it designates is not fanciful or arbitrary but rather arises from qualities, reputation or other characteristics which are attributable to its origin. The term “territory” means the locality, region, island, province, state or country where the goods originate; provided that such territory is identifiable and as indicated in the application for registration. An indication shall be deemed deceptively similar to a geographical indication registered if it so resembles the said mark as to likely cause confusion among consumers regarding the origin of the goods.

For the purposes of this Act, “good” means goods of agricultural origin including foodstuff, livestock, fish, wine and spirits, horticultural products, yarn and handloom fabrics. "Distinctiveness" with respect to a geographical indication registered shall mean that the connection between the good and the territory it designates is not fanciful or purely arbitrary but rather arises from qualities, reputation or other characteristics which are attributable to its origin. The term “territory” means the locality, region, island, province, state, country or combination thereof whose name serves to identify a geographical indication registered. A "producer" includes any person engaged in the production, processing, harvesting or preparation of goods originating from the territory specified in relation to the geographical indication registered.

For the purposes of this Act, an application for registration as a *geographical indication registered* may include a statement specifying existing trade marks used in relation to goods identical or similar to those produced under the proposed geographical indication. The Registrar shall consider any such statement and give due regard to the rights of the proprietor of the trade mark. Provided that the use of the geographical indication does not falsely suggest an association with, or endorsement by, the trade mark owner. Where a conflict arises between the protection afforded to a *geographical indication registered* and existing trademark rights, the Registrar shall determine the matter in accordance with principles of fairness and equity, balancing the interests of producers and consumers alike. The applicant shall furnish such evidence as the Registrar may require to substantiate the claim.

Where an application for registration of a *geographical indication registered* is filed, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish such evidence as he deems necessary to demonstrate that the quality, reputation, or characteristics of goods originate from the geographical territory specified in the application. Such evidence shall include verifiable data relating to agricultural practices, production methods, and processing techniques employed within the defined area. The applicant shall also provide a map clearly delineating the boundaries of the geographical unit. Any alteration to the registered *geographical indication* subsequent to registration requires prior approval from the Registrar, following a process of public notice and opportunity for objection regarding potential impact on existing users or trade mark rights. Registration is conditional upon continued compliance with these requirements.

For the purposes of this Act, "infringing copy" with respect to a work shall mean a reproduction of such work in any form whatsoever, including but not limited to its storage in any electronic medium. Such reproduction shall be deemed an infringing copy if it takes place without authorization or license from the owner of the copyright in that work, provided that fair dealing as defined elsewhere herein does not apply. An infringing copy includes copies made in contravention of conditions imposed by a contractual assignment of rights relating to the copyright. The term "reproduction" shall be interpreted broadly and encompasses any act which results in an identical or substantially similar version of the original work being created, subject to considerations of originality as determined under established legal principles.

For the purposes of this Act, an application for registration of copyright shall be deemed to provide prima facie evidence regarding the originality and authorship of the registered work. However, such registration does not preclude allegations that a subsequent reproduction constitutes an infringing copy if it can be demonstrated that the alleged infringer had knowledge of the substantial similarity between the copyrighted work and the reproduced material prior to its public presentation or distribution. The Registrar may, upon receiving credible evidence suggesting unauthorized duplication during the pendency of a copyright application, issue directives for investigation into potential infringement. Any determination regarding an infringing copy shall remain subject to judicial review based on established principles of copyright law.

For the purposes of this Act, an infringing copy shall be deemed to have been made where such reproduction, adaptation, or translation has occurred without due authorization from the copyright holder. Such authorization may take the form of a written license agreement explicitly granting rights for specified uses. Where an application for permission to utilize a copyrighted work is submitted and subsequently denied by the copyright owner, any subsequent act of copying shall be conclusively presumed to constitute infringement unless it can be demonstrated that such denial was obtained through fraudulent misrepresentation or undue coercion. The burden of proving compliance with conditions stipulated in a license agreement rests upon the party claiming authorization.

For the purposes of this Act, an "infringing copy" with respect to a work shall be deemed to include any reproduction thereof otherwise than under conditions specified by the copyright owner. Such reproduction may take the form of printing, writing, engraving, photographing or any other means whereby the work is capable of being perceived, reproduced or disseminated. An infringing copy also includes an adaptation that substantially reproduces the original work, irrespective of alterations made thereto. The determination of whether a copy constitutes an "infringing copy" shall be subject to consideration of the originality and creative expression embodied within the protected work. A record maintained in the Register of Copyrights shall serve as prima facie evidence regarding ownership claims relevant to establishing an infringing copy.

An application for rectification alleging non-use of a *design registered* shall be made to the Board within four years from the date of registration. The Board may entertain such an application only if it is satisfied that the applicant has taken reasonable steps to ascertain whether the alleged non-use occurred and that the design owner has been duly notified of the grounds for rectification, providing them a period not less than ninety days to respond. Should the Board find merit in the application after considering the response from the registered proprietor, it may direct cancellation of the registration or such other relief as deemed appropriate. The Board shall record its reasons for any order made under this provision and provide copies thereof to all parties involved.

Where an infringement of layout-design rights occurs following a successful challenge to the validity of a *design registered* before the Board, and where the aggrieved party can demonstrate substantial reliance on the now invalid registration in good faith when incurring damages, such as through investment in manufacturing processes or marketing campaigns, they shall be entitled to recover compensation from the proprietor whose actions led to the cancellation. This recovery may include not only direct pecuniary loss but also consequential losses reasonably foreseeable at the time of the infringement. Provided that any claim for compensation must be brought within three years from the date of publication of the Board’s order cancelling registration, and subject to proof satisfying the Court that the proprietor acted with knowledge or reckless disregard regarding the validity of the design.

An application for the registration of a layout-design shall be deemed abandoned if the applicant fails to comply with the requirements of sub-regulation (1) within six months from the date of receipt of the communication. The Board may, subject to just cause and after affording an opportunity of being heard to the applicant, revive such application notwithstanding the expiry of the aforementioned period. Where a layout-design is registered, any person who falsely represents that it is so registered shall be liable for penalty. The Central Government may, upon receiving representations from aggrieved parties concerning the validity of a design registered under this Act, initiate inquiries into potential infringements and consider appropriate remedial action.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings for infringement relating to a design registered with the Board, the court shall grant all remedies necessary to prevent further infringements and to compensate for past infringements.
