Such compensation may include damages sustained by the proprietor as a result of the infringing activity, taking into account any profits made by the infringer that were derived from the unauthorized use of the layout-design. The court may also order the destruction or disposal of goods embodying the infringing design. Further, where it is proven that an individual falsely represented a layout-design as being registered, they shall be liable to pay compensation to the proprietor and face penalties not exceeding two years imprisonment, subject to judicial discretion.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller, including orders relating to revocation, opposition, or sealing, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order. The Appellate Board shall consider such appeals and pass orders as it deems fit, subject to the provisions regarding costs which shall be determined in its discretion. Any party dissatisfied with an order passed by the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of receipt of the order. Failure to comply with these timelines shall render the appeal inadmissible. The Controller and the patent office are bound by decisions rendered by the Appellate Board, which have force as law.

The Controller may, at any time before the grant of a patent, require the applicant to furnish such further information or particulars as he deems necessary for the purpose of determining whether the invention is novel and involves an inventive step. Any request made under this provision shall be in writing and specify the grounds upon which it is based. The applicant shall have a period of ninety days from the date of receipt of such request within which to comply, failing which the application may be deemed abandoned. Where an amendment is proposed by the applicant pursuant to any direction issued by the patent office, the amended specification shall be treated as part of the original application for all purposes. The Controller shall record the reasons for allowing or rejecting any amendment.

An application for registration shall be deemed to be complete only upon submission of all prescribed forms, accompanied by the requisite fee as determined by the Controller. The applicant shall furnish a declaration verifying the accuracy and completeness of information provided within the application, affirming that no prior similar invention is currently registered or pending before any other patent office globally. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the registration request. Any alteration made to the submitted documents after initial receipt by the patent office necessitates a fresh fee payment and acknowledgement of amendment on each altered page. The Controller may, at his discretion, require further clarification or documentation from the applicant pertaining to any aspect of the invention described within the application for registration.

Where an applicant fails to comply with the requirements of this Act, or the regulations framed thereunder, relating to the form and content of the application, the Patent Office may afford such opportunity for amendment as it deems fit. Any amended document shall be deemed part of the original application only if filed within the prescribed time limit. Failure to rectify deficiencies identified by the Patent Office shall render the application liable for rejection. The Controller General may, at his discretion, require an applicant to furnish a certified copy of any relevant copyright registration pertaining to drawings or diagrams included in the patent application, provided such inclusion is deemed necessary for clarity and understanding of the invention. Any appeal against a decision of the Patent Office regarding amendment shall be made within sixty days.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, an indication specifying goods originating from a particular geographical area shall be deemed distinctive if it is capable of distinguishing those goods from other similar goods. The Registering Authority may require evidence demonstrating that the quality, reputation or characteristics of the goods are essentially attributable to the origin indicated. An application for registration may be opposed by any interested party within three months from the date of publication of the acceptance of the application in the Geographical Indications Journal. Such opposition shall specify the grounds on which it is based and shall be accompanied by a statement of particulars. The Registering Authority shall give notice of such opposition to the applicant, who may submit his reply or counter-statement.

For the purposes of this Act, “geographical indication” means an indication which identifies goods originating from a specific geographical area, where a quality, reputation, or other characteristic of those goods is essentially attributable to that origin. An indication may be deemed a geographical indication even if it does not directly denote the place name of origin, provided its use reasonably signifies such origin and connects the good with that locality. “Good” includes agricultural products, foodstuffs, wine, spirit, beverages, textiles, handicrafts, and manufactured goods. The Central Register shall maintain a publicly accessible register of all registered geographical indications. Any alteration to an existing geographical indication requires prior approval from the Registrar.

An application for registration as a geographical indication shall include particulars specifying the name of the geographical indication as it is proposed to be registered, a map of the area of its origin indicating clearly its boundaries, details establishing that the quality, reputation or other characteristic substantially associated with said territory. The applicant must provide evidence demonstrating continuous use of the geographical indication within the defined territorial limits for at least three years immediately preceding the date of application. Further, the Central Registry may require submission of additional documentation to verify authenticity and prevent fraudulent claims concerning the distinctiveness of the proposed geographical indications. Any alteration to the registered boundaries shall be subject to approval by the Registrar.

For the purposes of this Act, “geographical indication” means an indication which identifies goods as originating from a place or region where a particular quality, reputation, or other characteristic thereof is essentially attributable to its geographical origin. Such indications shall include signs that directly evoke the specified locality, or are otherwise indicative of it. An agricultural product may be considered to have a geographical indication even if production, processing, or preparation predominantly takes place in a single location within the defined territory. The Central Government may publish notifications relating to applications for registration and other matters concerning this Act in the Official Gazette. Any alteration to registered geographical indications shall also be published in the Official Gazette.

For the purposes of this Act, an agricultural product originating from a region specified in the register of Geographical Indications of Goods shall be deemed to bear that registered geographical indication if it is produced, processed and prepared within the defined geographical area as per documented traditional practices. Any person utilizing a sign purporting to be a registered geographical indication must demonstrate compliance with established quality control measures approved by the Registering Authority; failure to do so constitutes misrepresentation. The Registering Authority may require submission of detailed production records for verification purposes. Provided that, any prior use of a similar name or mark shall not invalidate registration if such use does not create confusion regarding origin and authenticity as assessed by the Geographical Indications Board.

For the purposes of this Act, “good quality” with relation to goods indicated by a registered geographical indication means that the goods conform to standards specified in regulations framed under this Act and are produced using traditional methods. "Distinctiveness" shall mean characteristics which identify such goods as originating from the territory named in the registration; provided that these characteristics are not common to similar goods originating from other territories. The term “territory of origin” means the region or locality within India, whose name constitutes the registered geographical indication and from whose products it originates. A "registered geographical indication" is deemed to be a mark capable of being exclusively used by authorized users in accordance with this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, an application for registration of a *registered geographical indication* shall include particulars relating to the growers’ associations or producers' collectives claiming benefit from such registration. The Central Government may require submission of documentation demonstrating collective control over production and quality standards relevant to the claimed geographical origin. Any alteration in these documented standards subsequent to the initial application must be reported to the Registrar within thirty days, accompanied by a reasoned justification for the change. Failure to comply with this reporting requirement shall render the registered proprietor liable to have their registration reviewed. The Central Government may also conduct periodic inspections of production areas and quality control processes to ensure continued adherence to prescribed standards.

Any person proposing to use a registered geographical indication in relation to goods for which it is protected shall ensure that such use complies with conditions specified by the Register. The Register may, after due notice and opportunity for hearing, impose further limitations on the permissible uses if it determines that continued protection of the registered geographical indication requires stricter controls. Any producer or trader who makes a false representation concerning the registration status of a product, claiming it possesses a protected characteristic attributable to a registered geographical indication, shall be liable for damages. Such representations must clearly indicate whether the goods originate from the area specified in the Register and adhere to quality standards as prescribed by the appropriate authority.

For the purposes of this Act, where a patent is granted to a *company*, the registration shall specify the registered office of that *company* as the place of incorporation. Any alteration in the location of the registered office of the *company* shall be notified to the Controller within thirty days of such change by way of an application accompanied by certified true copies of relevant resolutions passed by the Board of Directors and shareholders. The Controller may, upon receipt of such notification, update the records pertaining to the patent accordingly. Failure to notify the Controller as required herein shall render the *company* liable for a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable from the designated officer responsible for compliance with this Act.

Where an offence involving a violation of this Act is committed by a *company*, it shall be understood that every director, manager, secretary, and officer in default of the *company* at the time the offence was committed shall be deemed guilty of the act and liable to punishment as if he or she were the *company*. Provided that where the guilt of an individual is established, such individual shall not be excused from liability by reason only that they acted on behalf of a *company*, subject to demonstrating reasonable grounds for believing their actions were duly authorized. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify procedures for determining the identity of officers responsible for offences committed by a *company*.

For the purposes of this Act, where an invention is assigned to a *company*, and that assignment is recorded with the Controller in accordance with prescribed procedures, the liability for offences relating to false representation or suppression of material facts during the application process shall vest solely within the designated officer authorized by the company’s board of directors. This authorization must be evidenced by a certified resolution filed with the Controller prior to any action taken under this Act. Provided that, if such an offence is committed through demonstrable negligence on the part of an employee acting outside their prescribed authority, the *company* shall not be held liable unless it can be proven that reasonable due diligence was not exercised in selecting and supervising said employee. The Controller may require further documentation to ascertain compliance with these provisions.

For the purposes of this Act, where a patent is granted to a *company*, the obligation and liability for ensuring compliance with the terms of the grant, including payment of renewal fees and submission of prescribed forms, shall devolve upon that *company* as a body corporate. Any act or omission constituting an offence under this Act committed by such *company* shall be deemed to have been so committed by the acting director, manager, secretary, or any other officer responsible for the management of the affairs of the *company*, subject to their ability to demonstrate reasonable due diligence in preventing the infringement. The Central Government may issue notifications specifying procedures for serving notices and initiating proceedings against such officers where a *company* is found guilty of an offence.

For the purposes of this Act, “registered proprietor” includes any person who has obtained registration under the laws of a *convention country* and who claims priority from a patent application made in that country. Such registration shall be deemed equivalent to an Indian patent application for the purpose of assessing novelty and inventive step, subject to the provisions regarding grace periods as prescribed by the Regulations framed thereunder. An applicant claiming priority based on such foreign registration may submit certified copies thereof as evidence during examination proceedings. The Controller *may* require further documentation establishing the validity of the registered proprietor’s claim in the originating jurisdiction, provided that this requirement shall not prejudice the rights accrued to any party prior to the publication of the application in India.

For the purposes of this Act, “convention country” includes any state that is signatory to the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property. The term "convention country" shall be interpreted broadly and may include states which accede to the said Convention at a later date. An application for a patent derived from an earlier filing in a convention country shall be deemed a “convention application,” subject to compliance with prescribed formalities regarding priority dates and documentation as specified by regulations made under this Act. The benefit of an earlier filing date, where applicable, shall accrue only if the applicant furnishes a certified copy of the first application within the time limit stipulated herein. A patent granted based on a convention application is considered a patent for all purposes under this legislation.

For the purposes of this Act, “convention country” includes any state party to the Patent Cooperation Treaty and any nation designated by the Central Government under notification published in the Official Gazette. An application for registration shall be deemed to be a convention application if it complies with the requirements prescribed therein and is filed within twelve months from the date of filing an earlier related application in a convention country, subject to provisions regarding grace periods as determined by the Controller. Any act constituting infringement of a patent granted on the basis of a convention application shall be treated as having occurred not only in India but also deemed to have taken place in the convention country where the initial invention was first filed, for purposes of determining jurisdiction and applicable remedies.

For the purposes of registration, where an applicant seeks to register two or more trade marks such that they are deemed to be closely and substantially associated by reason of their identity or similarity in sound, appearance, meaning, or a combination thereof, the Registrar may direct that those trade marks shall be registered as *associated trade marks*. Such direction shall only be given after due consideration of any opposition filed under this Act. The applicant shall provide an affidavit detailing the rationale for seeking registration as associated trade marks and demonstrating the close connection between them. Any person aggrieved by a decision to register trade marks as associated may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision, following prescribed procedures.

For the purposes of registration, where an applicant seeks to register two or more trade marks such that they are deemed to be, or required to be, registered as associated trade marks, the application shall specify each trade mark proposed for association. The Trade Marks Registry may require the submission of a reasoned statement outlining the commercial rationale underlying the request for associated trade mark registration and demonstrating a clear connection between the goods or services indicated in relation to each trade mark. Such statement must detail how the use of the associated trade marks will not create confusion amongst consumers. Failure to provide such a statement, or provision of a deficient one as determined by the Registry, shall be grounds for rejection of the application. The Registrar may grant an extension of time for submission of this rationale.

For the purposes of registration, where an applicant seeks to register two or more trade marks relating to identical or similar goods or services as associated trade marks, the Registrar shall consider whether such association exists based on factors including common ownership, consistent marketing strategies, and a demonstrable consumer perception of interconnectedness. The application for registration of associated trade marks must clearly identify each mark involved in the association and specify the nature of that relationship. Any literary work incorporated within promotional materials accompanying the trademark application is subject to copyright law; however, such copyright does not affect the registrability of the trademarks themselves provided all necessary permissions are obtained. Failure to disclose relevant information regarding the associated trade marks may render the registration vulnerable to cancellation.

For the purposes of registration as associated trade marks, an application may be filed jointly by persons who are owners of distinct trade marks and desire to have those marks registered as being so associated. The Registrar shall consider such a joint application only if each applicant demonstrates that their respective trade mark has been in use for at least six months immediately preceding the date of the application. Further, the Registrar may require evidence establishing a commercial relationship between the applicants sufficient to warrant registration as associated trade marks. Any objection raised by a third party regarding the appropriateness of such association shall be adjudicated according to established procedures and principles applicable to oppositions under this Act.

Where an applicant files an application for invention relating to a process or composition, such application may be accompanied by a provisional specification describing the invention. The provisional specification need only disclose the matter which the inventor believes at the time would constitute the invention; however, it must provide a sufficient basis for claiming priority of the patent application. Failure to furnish a complete specification within twelve months from the date on which the provisional specification was first filed shall render the application liable for rejection. Any claim in the complete specification shall be restricted to matter disclosed in the provisional specification as originally filed, subject to any amendments permitted under this Act and the Rules made thereunder.

Where an applicant elects to file a provisional specification in conjunction with an application for patent protection, such provisional specification must satisfy requirements pertaining to enablement. The provisional specification shall disclose the invention sufficiently to enable a person skilled in the art to carry out the said invention. Further, any claims appended to a subsequent complete specification derived from a provisional specification are subject to scrutiny regarding their consistency with the disclosure contained within that initial provisional document. Should the claims extend beyond the scope of matter disclosed in the provisional specification, or fail to meet the enablement standard as applied to that earlier filing, they shall be deemed invalid. The applicant may amend the claims only to align them with the original provisional specification’s content.

Where an applicant submits a provisional specification along with an application for patent protection, such submission does not absolve them from subsequent obligations regarding claim clarity. The Controller may require amendments to claims within the complete specification, even if those claims relate directly to matter disclosed in the initial provisional document. Failure by the applicant to address these requirements within the prescribed timeframe shall render the application liable for rejection on grounds of insufficient disclosure or lack of enablement. Further, any rights accrued based solely upon representations made within a deficient provisional specification are subject to revocation should subsequent examination reveal material discrepancies from the complete specification filed thereafter.

Where an applicant elects to file a provisional specification in support of an application for invention, such provisional specification must contain a description sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art or technology to make and use the invention. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe guidelines regarding the format and content requirements applicable to provisional specifications. Failure to adhere to these prescribed guidelines shall render the provisional specification deficient for the purposes of this Act. An applicant submitting a provisional specification is deemed to have undertaken that all information disclosed therein will be incorporated into any subsequent complete specification filed relating to the same invention.

For the purposes of this Act, "visual recording" shall include any fixation in any medium—whether photographic, electronic, or otherwise—of moving images which are capable of being shown as a sequence of individual pictures creating the illusion of motion. Such recordings shall be deemed to constitute cinematograph films if they have been produced with the intention of commercial exhibition and meet technical standards prescribed by the Central Government through notification in the Official Gazette. Provided that, where a visual recording is primarily intended for private or domestic use without any element of public display or distribution, it shall not be considered a cinematograph film subject to such conditions as may be specified by regulations framed under this Act. The right of broadcast reproduction conferred upon the owner of a cinematograph film extends to copies made from such visual recordings.

For the purposes of this Act, "visual recording" shall mean any fixation in any medium—whether photographic, electronic, or otherwise—of one or more moving images which may be accompanied by sound. Such a visual recording includes but is not limited to motion picture films, video tapes, and digital recordings produced for broadcast or private exhibition. A compilation of still photographs arranged sequentially with the intention of conveying narrative or information shall also constitute a "visual recording" if such arrangement creates an illusion of movement. The term “visual recording” does not include works which are primarily literary or artistic in character, even where they incorporate moving images as incidental elements. Any alteration to a visual recording subsequent to its initial fixation shall be considered part of the original work for determining copyright ownership.

For the purposes of this Act, "visual recording" shall include any fixation in any material medium of a moving image or series of related images capable of continuous reproduction. A cinematographic film which incorporates elements generated wholly by computer and not derived from pre-existing works shall be deemed a work of visual recording for all purposes relating to copyright infringement. Provided that, where such a visual recording is prescribed as an educational resource by the Central Board of Secondary Education or any equivalent body recognized under law, copies made solely for bona fide classroom instruction are permissible without requiring prior authorization from the owner of the copyright in the film. The right to reproduce a broadcast embodying a work of visual recording shall be subject to conditions prescribed by the Copyright Advisory Board.

For the purposes of this Act, "visual recording" shall include any fixation in any medium of photographic images or sounds and such images or sounds. A person claiming copyright in a visual recording may apply to the Copyright Office for registration thereof; provided that such application shall be accompanied by certified copies of all scripts, dialogues, musical scores, lyrics, and other relevant materials used in the creation of the work. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all visual recordings so registered, accessible for public inspection subject to prescribed regulations concerning privacy and confidentiality. Any alteration or modification made to a registered visual recording subsequent to its initial registration requires notification to the Copyright Office within thirty days; failure to comply renders such alterations voidable.

For the purposes of this Act, “designated international office” means the International Bureau of the World Intellectual Property Organization. An “international registration,” when designating India, shall have effect only in respect of goods or services comprised within the list of goods and/or services specified therein at the time of such designation. "International application" includes an application filed under the Madrid Protocol concerning the International Registration of Marks; provided that any reference to ‘receiving office’ herein shall be construed as a reference to the Trade Marks Registry acting in that capacity, notwithstanding whether it is also designated as a “designated international office.” The registry may require such fees and provide such forms as are necessary for processing an international application.

For the purposes of this Act, an “international application” shall mean an application filed with the Trade Marks Registry under the Madrid Protocol concerning the International Registration of Marks. The Registry shall maintain a record of all international applications received and shall process them in accordance with the provisions of the Protocol and any rules made thereunder. Any request for modification or renewal relating to an international registration, including but not limited to changes to ownership details or indication of goods and services, may be filed directly with the Trade Marks Registry. The Registrar may require such documentation as is necessary to verify compliance with Indian trade mark law in relation to an international application. Examination shall proceed subject to any priority claims arising from earlier applications.

For the purposes of this Act, an international application shall be deemed to have been filed at the Trade Marks Registry on the date it is received by the International Bureau and transmitted to the Office. The Registrar shall deal with such applications in accordance with the Convention relating to the Madrid Administration of marks and any rules made thereunder. Where an international application designates India, the prescribed fees for examination and registration shall be payable as if the application were a domestic application. Provided that, where the applicant is unable to comply with the prescribed fee payment schedule due to circumstances beyond their control, they may apply for condonation of delay accompanied by a duly verified affidavit explaining the reasons for non-compliance.

For the purposes of this Act, “international application” includes any application filed with the Trade Marks Registry under the provisions of the Madrid Protocol concerning the International Registration of Marks, and shall be deemed to be an application for registration within the meaning of this Act. An international application is considered complete upon receipt by the Registry, provided that all required fees have been duly paid as per regulations prescribed by the Board. The Registry may request further information or clarification from the applicant relating to such an international application. Any designation in respect of India contained in an international application shall be treated as a separate and distinct application for registration.

The Geographical Indications Registry shall maintain registers for the purpose of recording applications for registration and particulars relating thereto. Applications received by the Registry shall be examined in accordance with prescribed procedures, and any objections raised against an application shall be promptly communicated to the applicant, providing a reasonable opportunity for response or modification. The Registrar may require applicants to furnish such documentary evidence as is deemed necessary to substantiate claims of origin and distinctiveness associated with the proposed geographical indication. Information pertaining to registered geographical indications, including details of proprietors and conditions of use, shall be made available for public inspection at the Registry office during normal business hours. Any alteration or amendment to a register entry must be recorded in writing and authenticated by an officer authorized by the Registrar.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Geographical Indications Registry relating to the registration of a geographical indication, or the rectification of the register, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeals shall be filed within sixty days from the date on which the order is communicated to the appellant. The Board may, in its discretion, entertain appeals lodged after the expiry of the said period if it is satisfied that the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause from filing the appeal within the prescribed time. Decisions of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board shall be final subject to further appeal under the provisions of the relevant appellate jurisdiction act. Costs relating to such proceedings may be awarded at the discretion of the Board.

For the purposes of this Act, “registered Geographical Indication” means an indication which has been registered in the Register maintained by the Geographical Indications Registry and in respect of which a certificate of registration has been granted; "owner" with reference to a geographical indication, includes any association or cooperative society engaged in production and processing of goods conforming to a particular quality, reputation or other characteristic attributed to that territory originating from it; “distinctiveness” means the capability of a sign to distinguish goods as being geographically linked to a specific region, town, locality, or area; "the Register" means the register maintained by the Geographical Indications Registry for the registration of geographical indications. The Controller may require such modifications of an application as are necessary for its proper examination and determination.

The Geographical Indications Registry shall maintain a public record of all applications for registration and registrations made under this Act. This record shall include, but not be limited to, particulars relating to the name of the geographical indication, the goods or services it relates to, the registered proprietor, and any limitations or conditions attached to the registration. The Registrar may require applicants to provide such further information as is necessary for the proper examination of an application. Any person interested in a pending application before the Geographical Indications Registry may inspect the relevant file subject to regulations prescribed by the Central Government. Details of successful registrations shall be published in the Official Gazette and made available online.

For the purposes of this Act, “convention application” shall be deemed to include any application for a patent filed in a designated convention country by the applicant or their legal representative within six months preceding the date of filing the subsequent application in India. Such applications shall be accompanied by certified true copies of the earlier application and its claims as originally filed. The Controller may require further documentation substantiating the priority claim, including declarations from authorized officials of the receiving office. An application claiming priority under a convention application is subject to examination for compliance with all procedural requirements applicable at the time of filing in India; provided that any deficiency shall be notified to the applicant within three months and an opportunity afforded for rectification.

For the purposes of this Act, “convention application” shall be deemed to include any application for a patent filed in a designated convention country by the applicant or their legal representative within six months preceding the date of filing the subsequent application in India. Such applications shall be accompanied by certified true copies of the earlier application and its claims as originally filed. The Controller may require further documentation substantiating the priority claim, including declarations from authorized officials of the receiving office. An applicant claiming benefit of a convention application shall furnish an address for service in India, subject to the provisions regarding registered patent agents. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the application liable for rejection on grounds of non-compliance.

For the purposes of this Act, “convention application” shall be deemed to be an application for a patent that claims priority from a prior application made in a Convention Country. Such applications must adhere strictly to the prescribed form detailed within the register maintained by the Controller and shall include certified copies of the earlier filing as evidence of priority claim. The particulars relating to such convention applications, including dates of earliest filings and applicant details, are subject to public inspection upon request. Any discrepancies between the information presented in a convention application and the corresponding record in the register may be rectified at the discretion of the Controller after due notice is provided to all affected parties.

Where a person making a convention application has, prior to the date of the application, applied for protection of the invention in a convention country, and such earlier application contains drawings which are substantially similar to those accompanying the convention application, the Controller may require that copies of said drawings be deposited with the office. Failure to comply with this requirement within the time specified shall render the application liable to rejection. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this provision may appeal to the Appellate Board. The copyright in any reproductions of such drawings prepared for the purposes of compliance remains vested in the applicant, subject to the Controller’s right to use them for official purposes.

An application for registration of a *registered layout* shall be accompanied by such particulars and documents as may be prescribed. The Office shall furnish an acknowledgment containing its date of receipt to the applicant. Upon examination, if the Registrar finds that the layout-design is capable of being registered under this Act, he shall publish a notification in the Official Gazette inviting objections from any person within three months from the date of publication. Any objection received after the expiry of said period may be disregarded. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit further information or modifications to clarify aspects of the layout-design’s novelty and originality before proceeding with registration, subject to compliance with prescribed timelines.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall include particulars specifying the name and address of the applicant, a representation of the layout-design conforming to prescribed standards, and a statement affirming that the layout-design has not been previously registered in India. The Director General may reject an application if it is found to be deficient in any material respect or does not comply with the requirements outlined in the regulations framed under this Act. Where the applicant fails to rectify deficiencies within the time specified by the Director General, the application shall stand rejected. Upon successful completion of examination and verification, a *registered layout* will be entered into the Register of Layout-Designs maintained as per procedures detailed therein.

Where any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar relating to the registration or rejection of a registered layout, or concerning rectification of entries in the Register of Layout-Designs, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Appellate Board may, after giving notice to all concerned parties and affording them an opportunity for being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. Any decision of the Appellate Board shall be final subject to further appeal under the provisions governing appeals to higher courts. Failure to comply with this process constitutes a bar to seeking any remedy in respect of the matter.

An application for registration of a *registered layout* shall contain particulars verifying ownership and detailing the circuit configuration. The applicant must provide certified copies of all relevant documentation establishing prior rights or licenses pertaining to the layout design. Where an existing *register* entry reveals identical or substantially similar features, the Controller may require submission of comparative analyses demonstrating novelty and originality. Registration is conditional upon compliance with prescribed standards for clarity and precision in depicting the integrated circuit’s structure. The applicant shall confirm that all elements within the layout-design are either wholly original or subject to appropriate permissions from relevant rights holders. Failure to satisfy these conditions will result in rejection of the application, provided that the Controller provides written justification for such a determination.

Subject to compliance with prescribed formalities and payment of requisite fees as determined by the Copyright Board, an individual seeking authorization to produce and publish translations shall submit a detailed proposal outlining the intended language conversion and target audience. The proposer must demonstrate reasonable efforts have been undertaken to ascertain the copyright holder’s contact information and provide evidence thereof or satisfy the Board that such attempts proved unsuccessful despite diligent inquiry. Furthermore, where the original work is subject to an existing licence restricting reproduction rights, the proposed translation shall not contravene those limitations. Any publication of translations without prior authorization from the Copyright Board renders the publisher liable for statutory penalties and injunctive relief.

For the purposes of this Act, "translation" with reference to any literary or dramatic work shall mean reproduction thereof in another language by means of interpretation, rendering, or adaptation. The right to control the publication of translations is vested in the owner of copyright in the original work, subject to the provisions herein relating to compulsory licensing. Any person seeking authorization to produce and publish a translation shall be deemed to apply for a licence from the copyright proprietor. Such application must specify the original work, the language into which it is proposed to be translated, and the intended mode of publication. The term "publish translations" includes making available such translations in any form accessible to the public, whether by sale, hire, or other means.

Any individual seeking authorization to produce and publish translations shall submit an application to the Controller of Copyrights, detailing the original work’s title, author, country of origin, and language of the proposed translation. The application must be accompanied by certified copies of registration documents pertaining to the copyright in the original work, or evidence demonstrating due diligence undertaken to ascertain ownership. Where the design elements incorporated within an illustrative component of the original work are subject to separate intellectual property protection, a declaration confirming compliance with relevant regulations concerning such designs shall also be included. The Controller may require further documentation and may conduct hearings before issuing a determination regarding the application’s merits.

For the purposes of this Act, “translation” with reference to a literary or artistic work shall mean reproduction of the work in another language by means of an interpretation of the original. A "published translation" is defined as a translation of any work wherein copies have been offered for sale or otherwise distributed to the public. The right to produce and publish translations of works is subject to the provisions relating to compulsory licences, provided that such publication shall not be deemed infringing upon the existing copyright in the original work unless specifically authorized by the owner of said copyright. Any person seeking authorization to publish a translation must demonstrate reasonable efforts were made to obtain consent from the rights holder prior to application.

For the purposes of this Act, “legal representative” with regard to any deceased applicant for a patent, or deceased inventor where such inventor is also an applicant, shall include the executor or administrators of the estate of that person duly appointed and acting under the authority of law. Such legal representative shall possess all rights and be subject to all obligations which the deceased would have had if living. Where an application has been made jointly by two or more persons, the “legal representative” shall include the legal representatives of any such joint applicants. The term "legal representative" also extends to a person lawfully authorized under applicable law to administer the intellectual property rights of another individual who is incapacitated and unable to act on their own behalf.

For the purposes of this Act, where an applicant for patent is a minor or of unsound mind, or dies before grant of the patent, any application made by such applicant may be continued and prosecuted by their legal representative. The term "legal representative" with respect to a deceased applicant shall include his executor or administrator duly appointed under the applicable law relating to succession; provided that such executor or administrator furnishes satisfactory proof of appointment and authority to act on behalf of the estate, as prescribed by the Controller. Further, where an application is assigned, the legal representative of the assignor shall be deemed to have transferred all rights and title in respect of the patent to the assignee, subject to any outstanding obligations under the assignment agreement.

For the purposes of this Act, where an applicant for a patent, or the registered proprietor of a patent, is a minor or of unsound mind, any act required to be done by such applicant or proprietor may be lawfully performed by their legal representative duly appointed and authorised under law. The Controller shall not entertain any application or communication unless it is established that the person executing the same is indeed the legal representative acting on behalf of the aforementioned individual, supported by appropriate documentation as prescribed by regulations framed thereunder. Provided that, in cases where a legal representative seeks to relinquish their authority, such relinquishment must be formally notified to the Controller and acknowledged in writing.

For the purposes of this Act, “legal representative” with regard to an applicant for a patent, or a patentee, shall include the duly appointed executor or administrator of their estate, and any person lawfully authorised under applicable law to administer property belonging to such deceased individual. Where an application for a patent is filed by an individual, and that individual subsequently dies prior to grant, the legal representative may continue with the proceedings in place of the deceased applicant, subject to providing satisfactory evidence of appointment to the Controller. The particulars of any such legal representative shall be entered into the register maintained under this Act, alongside the relevant application or patent details, and subsequent correspondence relating thereto shall be addressed accordingly.

For the purposes of this Act, an exclusive licence shall be deemed to have been granted where a patentee conveys to another party the right to exploit a patented invention within the territory of India, subject to the condition that such exploitation is restricted solely to the licensee and that no other person has been authorized by the patentee to perform acts falling within the scope of the claim. The record of any such exclusive licence shall be filed with the Controller, specifying the duration of exclusivity, geographical limitations, and a detailed description of the rights granted. Failure to file this record within three months from the date of grant of the license will render the exclusivity ineffective against third parties. Any modification or termination of an existing exclusive licence must also be recorded in like manner.

Where an exclusive licence is granted under this Act, the patentee shall retain all rights not expressly conferred upon the licensee. The terms of such licences may specify royalties payable to the licensee, which shall be determined by agreement between the parties or, in cases of dispute, as prescribed by the Controller. Failure by the licensee to adhere to the agreed royalty structure constitutes a breach of contract and renders them liable for damages sustained by the patentee. Further, any assignment of rights granted under an exclusive licence requires prior written consent from the original patentee, subject to judicial review if deemed necessary to protect the public interest in promoting innovation. The Controller may inquire into the reasonableness of licensing terms upon complaint filed by an aggrieved party.

For the purposes of this Act, an “exclusive licence” shall mean a licence granted in respect of a patent, conferring upon the licensee the sole right to make, use, exercise, sell, offer for sale, or import the patented invention within the territory of India, subject to the conditions specified therein. Such exclusive licences may be granted by the patentee either wholly or partially, and may relate to one or more fields of use of the invention. An exclusive licence shall not extend beyond the term of the patent unless expressly provided for in the agreement granting such licence. The grant of an exclusive licence does not prejudice any rights subsisting under copyright law relating to drawings, designs, or other artistic works incorporated within the patented invention.

For the purposes of this Act, an exclusive licence shall be deemed to grant to the licensee the right solely to make, use, exercise, sell, offer for sale, and import the patented invention within the territory of India, subject to the terms specified in the license agreement. Such agreements may stipulate limitations on field of use or quantity sold; however, any act performed by or on behalf of the exclusive licensee that constitutes an infringement of the patent holder’s rights prior to the grant of the licence shall be deemed a matter for consideration during subsequent proceedings relating to validity and enforceability. The Controller may require registration of such licences with prescribed fees and forms, providing public record of the assignment and its conditions.

Any person aggrieved by an entry in the registers relating to a design may institute proceedings seeking relief, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Such proceedings shall be brought before the Controller within six months from the date on which such entry was made or became apparent. The Controller may order rectification of the registers if it is satisfied that the entry is erroneous or contrary to law; provided that any application for rectification alleging newly discovered facts must be supported by an affidavit verifying their truthfulness. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements shall render the proceedings void, and no compensation shall be awarded in respect of such dismissal. The Controller’s order regarding rectification shall be final, subject to appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of thirty days.

Applications for entry into the registers relating to designs shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee, payable to the Controller. The Controller may require applicants to furnish further particulars concerning the design and its intended use; failure to comply within the stipulated timeframe will render the application liable for rejection. Any person claiming an interest in a registered design may petition the Controller requesting rectification of the registers if they allege errors or omissions affecting their rights, subject to demonstrating sufficient cause and providing supporting documentation as determined by the Controller. The register shall be deemed conclusive evidence of registration unless proven otherwise before a competent judicial authority. No trust relating to any right conferred under this Act shall be entered in the registers.

The Controller may, at any time, require the Registrar to amend the registers relating to designs where it appears that an entry is erroneous or otherwise prejudicial to the interests of a design owner. Any alteration made pursuant to such requirement shall be recorded with the reasons for the amendment and signed by the Controller’s authorized representative. The register maintained under this Act shall be deemed public documents, subject to restrictions imposed regarding confidential information disclosed during registration proceedings. An application for entry in the registers may include details of any trusts affecting ownership; however, no notice of such trust shall be entered into the registers themselves, and the Controller is not bound to inquire into the validity or extent of any such interest.

Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the entry of any matter into the registers maintained under this Act may appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date on which such decision is communicated to him. The Controller shall consider all relevant materials and, subject to just cause shown, may allow or dismiss the appeal. Where an application for registration contains particulars that are false or misleading, or where a registered design has been obtained through fraud, any person claiming title adverse to the registered proprietor may apply to the Controller for rectification of the registers. The Controller shall afford both parties an opportunity to be heard before making any order affecting the validity of the registration.

The Authority may, upon receipt of an application for registration of a variety, direct the applicant to furnish further information or submit additional propagating material deemed necessary for assessment. Any request made under this provision shall specify the nature and quantity of the required materials or details. Failure by the applicant to comply with such direction within the time specified will render the application liable to rejection. The Registrar shall maintain an updated record of all applications, including those withdrawn or rejected, accessible for public inspection subject to prescribed fees. A *registered variety* confers upon the breeder exclusive rights relating to the production and sale of propagating material derived from that variety, provided that such propagation does not constitute farm exempt use as defined in this Act.

The Authority may, upon receipt of an application for registration under this Act, conduct such inquiries as it deems necessary to ascertain whether the variety possesses characteristics that are demonstrably new and stable. An applicant shall furnish a detailed description of the plant material comprising the *registered variety*, including its botanical name, lineage where known, and distinctive features observable across generations. The Authority may require submission of propagating material for examination at a designated institution. Any person claiming rights in relation to a previously registered variety must disclose all relevant prior art pertaining to that line of development. Failure to comply with these disclosure requirements shall render the application liable for rejection.

Where a person alleges that any act has been committed which infringes rights relating to a *registered variety*, they may institute proceedings before an adjudicating officer appointed by the Central Government. Such proceedings shall be conducted according to principles of natural justice and evidence presented shall pertain directly to the alleged infringing activity, including unauthorized cultivation or dissemination of propagating material derived from the registered variety. The adjudicating officer may order remedies including injunctions preventing further infringement, compensation for damages sustained as a result of the infringement, and in cases of willful violation, impose penalties not exceeding five times the value of the infringing goods or services. Appeals against orders of the adjudicating officer lie to an appellate authority established under this Act.

An application for registration as a *registered variety* shall include detailed information regarding the genetic composition of the applicant’s material, including pedigree data where available. The Authority may require submission of additional documentation pertaining to stability and distinctiveness over successive generations. Where an application relates to a plant variety derived from another, the source variety must be clearly identified, along with evidence demonstrating substantial derivation. Any modification or alteration made to propagating material submitted in support of an *application* shall immediately invalidate that portion of the record. The Registrar may, at any time, require further information relating to the characteristics and expression of traits for assessment purposes.

For the purposes of this Act, a certification trade mark shall be defined as a mark that specifies compliance by goods or services with a particular standard, specification, characteristic, quality, original guarantee, production method, or other attribute. The use of such a mark shall require prior approval from an authority prescribed by regulations framed under this Act and continued adherence to the approved standards. Any person seeking to utilize a certification trade mark must demonstrate that they are authorized to do so by the relevant certifying body. Provided that the certifying body operates impartially and without any vested interest in the production or supply of the certified goods or services, its designation shall be deemed valid for the purposes of this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,—(a) "guarantee" with reference to a certification trade mark shall mean a guarantee that the goods or services specified in relation to such mark satisfy particular requirements; (b) “certification trade mark” means a trade mark which is used to signify to the public that the goods or services in connection with which it is used conform to a defined standard, specification or characteristic and is so used subject to conditions guaranteeing and controlling its use; (c) "certifier" means any body corporate or individual authorized by the Registrar to grant certification under this Act; (d) “specified requirements” includes characteristics relating to quality, production methods, origin, mode of manufacture or other particular attributes of goods or services. The Registrar may prescribe guidelines for determining whether specified requirements are met.

For the purposes of this Act, a certification trade mark shall denote a mark prescribed for exclusive use by an authorized body certifying conformity of goods or services to a specified standard, quality characteristic, or other attribute. Such authorization shall be granted only if the applicant demonstrates adherence to transparent and verifiable procedures ensuring impartiality in assessment. The Central Government may, after due inquiry, revoke such authorization if it determines that the authorized body is not functioning in accordance with its stated objectives or has engaged in practices detrimental to consumer interests. Use of a certification trade mark shall be restricted to goods or services meeting the prescribed criteria, subject to compliance audits conducted periodically by the authorized body and reported to the Central Government.

Subject to any other provision contained within this Act and without prejudice to the rights of licensees, a patentee shall be entitled to take legal proceedings against any person infringing their *patent rights*. Such infringement includes but is not limited to acts involving the unauthorized making, use, or sale of the patented invention. The patentee may seek an injunction restraining the infringer from continuing such actions and damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the patentee as a direct result of the infringement. Provided that where the infringing act was committed innocently, the Court may reduce the amount of damages awarded. Further, any party aggrieved by an action taken under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such action.

Subject to any other provision contained within this Act and without prejudice to the provisions of subsection (2), where a patent has been granted, the patentee shall be entitled to take proceedings for infringement relating to the patented invention. Any person who after the grant of a patent infringes such patent shall be liable to pay damages or an account of profits together with interest at such rate as may be prescribed. The Controller may, upon application by the patentee, determine whether any act constitutes an infringement and may issue orders restraining further acts of infringement. Provided that nothing in this provision shall prevent the use of a patented invention for purposes solely connected with the examination or determination of the validity of a patent or for the purpose of contesting its revocation. The exercise of such *patent rights* is subject to judicial review.

Subject to compliance with prescribed regulatory filings and adherence to quality control standards as determined by the Central Government, patent rights granted under this Act shall empower the patentee to exercise exclusive privileges regarding the invention’s manufacture, application, and commercial distribution within India. Provided that such exclusivity is contingent upon demonstrable evidence of ongoing substantial manufacturing operations undertaken in India relating to the patented invention, or a commitment to initiate said operations within a timeframe stipulated by the Central Government. Further, any assignment or transfer of patent rights shall be registered with the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trademarks, and deemed invalid if such registration is not secured within ninety days from the date of agreement.

Subject to any modifications directed by the Controller during examination, and provided that the prescribed fees are duly paid, registration of a patent shall vest definitively upon the date specified in the Patent Register. Such registration grants to the applicant, now declared as the patentee, exclusive rights within India relating to the invention claimed. These patent rights extend to preventing any person from making, using or importing the patented article without authorization. The Controller may, at any time after registration and following due process, require submission of evidence demonstrating adequate working of the patented invention in India; failure to provide such evidence shall be grounds for review of the validity of the patent’s registration.

The right to use a trade mark, whether registered or not, may be transmitted by assignment or otherwise, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated therein. Where such transmission relates to an unregistered trade mark used in connection with goods or services, the assignor shall remain liable for any infringement committed prior to the date of the transmission. Any subsequent owner acquiring a trade mark through operation of will or succession shall be deemed to have acquired all rights and obligations pertaining to the mark as if they were the original proprietor. The Registrar may require proof satisfactory to them regarding the validity of such transmissions, including documentation establishing the legal basis for the transfer and consent from any relevant third parties with an interest in the trade mark’s use.

For the purposes of this Act, a trade mark registered under this Act may be transmitted by assignment or otherwise, subject to the provisions herein. Any instrument effecting such transmission shall be executed with the same formality and authentication as is required for the transfer of immovable property under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. The Registrar shall not register any claim of title arising from a purported transmission unless satisfactory evidence thereof, including an authenticated copy of the relevant instrument, is furnished to the Registrar within thirty days of the date of execution. Failure to provide such evidence may render the claimed right unenforceable against the Registrar or third parties deriving rights under this Act. The burden of proving valid transmission shall rest upon the claimant.

For the purposes of this Act, “transmission” with respect to a trade mark registration shall include not only assignment by written instrument signed and attested as prescribed, but also devolution by operation of law, whether through succession or otherwise. Where a registered proprietor dies leaving a will, the benefit of the said registration, including all rights pertaining thereto, may be transmitted to any beneficiary named in such will; provided that if no will exists, transmission shall vest in the legal heirs and successors of the deceased proprietor according to applicable laws relating to intestate succession. The Registrar may require proof satisfactory to him regarding the validity of any claim for transmission before registering a new proprietor.

The right to use a trade mark, whether registered or not, may be transmitted by assignment or otherwise, subject to the provisions of this Act. Where such transmission occurs relating to a registered trade mark, the record thereof shall be updated within thirty days of intimation received from the assignor and assignee. The Registrar shall require evidence satisfactory to him establishing the validity of the instrument effecting the transmission and may refuse registration if he has reason to believe that the transmission is fraudulent or otherwise unlawful. Any person acquiring title to a trade mark by way of succession, whether testamentary or intestate, shall be deemed to have received the right subject to any encumbrances noted in the register.

Where, in proceedings before the Controller or any other authority under this Act, it is alleged that a claim lacks unity of invention, the patentee shall be afforded an opportunity to amend the claims to secure such unity. If the amendment substantially alters the nature of the claimed *invention*, the Controller may direct that a fresh examination take place as if the application were newly filed. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this provision relating to lack of unity may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final, subject to further appeal only on grounds specified in the relevant provisions concerning appeals from orders of the Controller. Costs incident to such appeal shall be determined by the Appellate Board.

For the purposes of this Act, an *invention* shall be deemed not to include a mere discovery of a known substance existing in nature. An application for patent relating to such a discovery may be filed with the Controller; however, the Controller shall require the applicant to demonstrate, through documented experimentation and verifiable data, that the claimed process or product involves a transformation resulting in an enhancement of the inherent properties of the discovered substance. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence as prescribed by the Regulations framed under this Act will result in rejection of the application. The burden of proving such transformation lies entirely upon the applicant. Any appeal against such rejection shall be made within three months from the date of communication of the order.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, an *invention* shall be deemed to include a new chemical entity where such entity exhibits demonstrable and reproducible utility in relation to a specified process or product. The Controller-General may require submission of detailed manufacturing protocols alongside application documentation demonstrating novelty and non-obviousness relative to existing prior art. Where the claimed invention incorporates elements derived from previously registered designs, an explicit declaration outlining these derivations shall be appended to the registration form. Any unauthorized manufacture, use, or sale of a patented *invention* following its registration constitutes infringement, subject to provisions regarding experimental use permitted solely for research purposes and not for commercial exploitation.

Where, in proceedings before the Controller or any other authority under this Act, it is alleged that an asserted *invention* infringes upon a copyright subsisting in any literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work, the burden shall lie upon the claimant alleging such infringement to demonstrate with reasonable certainty the substantial similarity between the claimed invention and the copyrighted material. Failure to satisfy this evidentiary threshold shall render the claim of non-infringement conclusive for the purposes of that proceeding. Any order restraining the manufacture, use, or sale of an invention based solely on a copyright allegation may be appealed to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Controller may award costs against any party found to have brought frivolous claims relating to copyright infringement.

Where a trade mark is registered, and it appears to the satisfaction of the court that infringement has occurred or is threatened, the court may grant an ex parte injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of infringement. Such injunction shall be granted only if the plaintiff demonstrates a reasonable likelihood of success in establishing their claim and provides security for costs as determined by the court. Provided that, where the alleged infringing activity involves substantial investment or widespread distribution, the court may consider factors including consumer confusion and dilution of distinctiveness when assessing the balance of convenience. The injunction shall be subject to such terms as the Court deems just and equitable, ensuring a fair outcome while protecting the registered trade mark owner’s rights.

Where a trade mark is registered, and it appears to the satisfaction of the court that infringement has occurred or is threatened, the court may grant an ex parte injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of infringement. Such injunction shall be granted only if the plaintiff demonstrates a reasonable likelihood of success in establishing their claim and provides security for costs as determined by the court. Provided that, where the alleged infringing activity involves substantial investment or widespread distribution, the court may consider factors including consumer confusion and dilution of the trade mark’s distinctiveness when assessing the necessity of an ex parte order. The defendant shall be afforded a prompt opportunity to challenge the injunction upon notice.

Where a trade mark is infringed, the Court may grant such relief as it deems just and equitable, including, but not limited to, an injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of infringement. In cases where the infringement has occurred ex parte, without notice to the registered proprietor, and demonstrable irreparable harm results therefrom, the Court shall consider granting a temporary or interim injunction pending determination of the merits of the suit. The terms of any such injunction may be prescribed by the Court to ensure fairness between the parties. Provided that the defendant demonstrates reasonable grounds for believing their actions did not constitute infringement, the Court may require the plaintiff to furnish security as deemed appropriate before an ex parte injunction is enforced.

Where a trade mark is registered, and it appears to the court that infringement has occurred, or is threatened, the court may grant an ex parte injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of infringement pending determination of the suit. Such injunction shall be granted only if the plaintiff demonstrates a prima facie case establishing ownership of the trade mark and reasonable apprehension of irreparable injury resulting from continued use by the defendant. The order for such ex parte injunction may include conditions requiring the plaintiff to provide security, as determined appropriate by the court, ensuring compensation should the injunction ultimately prove unwarranted or excessive upon full consideration of all evidence presented.

For the purposes of registration, an association seeking to register a collective mark shall submit detailed regulations governing its use. These regulations must specify the conditions for eligibility of members utilizing the mark and prescribe procedures ensuring uniformity in quality, characteristics, or geographical origin of goods or services indicated thereby. The Registrar may require amendments to these regulations if they are deemed insufficiently precise or fail to adequately safeguard the integrity of the collective mark. Further, any member found to have used the collective mark in a manner inconsistent with the approved regulations shall be subject to disciplinary action as prescribed by the association’s bylaws and may face revocation proceedings initiated by the Registrar.

For the purposes of this Act, "collective mark" means a sign adopted exclusively to distinguish the origin or quality or other characteristics, such as production method or distinctive features, of goods collectively marketed by its members or other persons who, subject to any conditions and limitations prescribed in the regulations framed under this Act, are authorized to use the said mark. Such authorization shall be governed by an agreement specifying the purposes for which the collective mark may be used and the conditions governing such use. The agreement must also define eligibility criteria for membership and outline procedures for maintaining uniformity of quality or characteristics relating to goods bearing the collective mark. Any alteration to the collective mark requires consent from all members, as per the regulations.

For the purposes of this Act, a collective mark shall signify a mark adopted by an association of persons engaged in producing identical goods or providing identical services. The registration of such a mark shall be subject to proof satisfactory to the Registrar that the applicant is a genuine and functioning association representing those producers or service providers. Further, the Central Government may, at any time, require the collective mark proprietor to furnish evidence demonstrating continued adherence to quality standards or production methods as stipulated in the application for registration; failure to do so shall render the mark liable for removal from the Register. The Registrar is empowered to issue directions regarding the use and control of the collective mark by members of the association.

For the purposes of registration and subsequent use, a collective mark shall represent an association of persons engaged in a particular commerce, industry, or profession. The Registrar may prescribe conditions governing eligibility for membership within such an association; provided that these prescribed conditions must demonstrably relate to maintaining quality standards or ensuring adherence to specific production methods relevant to the goods or services indicated by the mark. Any alteration to the composition of the association, including additions or removals of members, shall be reported to the Registrar within thirty days of the change taking effect. Further, use of the collective mark is conditional upon continued compliance with the prescribed conditions and active participation in the activities of the association.

For the purposes of this Act, a “composite mark” is defined as a mark consisting of elements which are capable of being separately recognised and reproduced. Where such composite mark is registered, the Registrar shall record that it comprises distinct parts, each part possessing its own distinctive character. The proprietor of a *marks registered* as a composite mark may elect to exercise rights pertaining only to one or more of those constituent parts, subject to due notice being given in any proceeding relating to infringement. Any use of a component element without the remainder of the composite mark shall not be deemed an infringing act if such use does not create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods or services. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating distinctiveness for each part of a registered composite mark during renewal proceedings.

The Registrar may, upon application by the owner of a mark registered prior to this Act coming into force, direct that any subsequent mark also be entered on the Register of Trade Marks as an associated trade mark. Such direction shall only be granted if the applicant demonstrates a continuous and substantial connection between the goods or services in relation to which each *marks registered* pertains. The Registrar is empowered to require evidence satisfactory to demonstrate this connection, including but not limited to contractual agreements, marketing materials, and sales figures. Any party aggrieved by such direction may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of notification of the decision. The Board’s determination shall be final subject to further appeal under the provisions governing appeals from that body.

For the purposes of this Act, a “composite mark” is defined as a mark consisting of elements which are capable of being separately recognised and reproduced. Where such composite mark is registered, the proprietor shall be entitled to enforce the rights conferred by the registration not only for the composite mark taken as a whole but also in relation to any element thereof, provided that such element is distinctive or has acquired distinctiveness through use following the date of registration of the composite mark. Nothing in this Act shall prevent the proprietor of a registered trade mark from acquiring patent protection for features incorporated within a registered mark, irrespective of whether those features are functional or aesthetic. The rights accruing to the owner of marks registered under this Act extend only to goods and services as specified in the register.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, any application claiming inventive step relating to a method for producing a substance shall specify with particularity the composition of said substance. Where such application relates directly or indirectly to a *patented article*, the applicant shall furnish an affidavit verifying that all prior art disclosures pertaining to the underlying invention have been duly considered and accounted for in the claims submitted. Failure to provide this verification, or providing a false verification, renders the registration liable to cancellation by the Controller. The Controller may require further documentation demonstrating freedom to operate with respect to any existing patents relevant to the claimed method of production before proceeding with examination.

Where any infringement of a patent has occurred, the right to claim damages shall accrue from the date of such infringement. The Controller may, upon application by the patentee, determine the extent of damage caused by the infringing activity, taking into consideration the loss of profits suffered by the patentee as a result thereof and the unreasonable profit gained by the infringer. Subject to appeal under this Act, any sum so determined shall be recoverable from the infringer as a debt due to the patentee.
