Where an injunction has been granted restraining infringement, subsequent damages may include compensation for losses arising after the date of the order granting such injunction. The term "patented article" includes not only articles made by application of the patented process but also those produced directly from the substance protected by the patent.

For the purposes of this Act, “biopharmaceutical product” shall include any therapeutic protein, peptide, nucleic acid, antibody, or other biologically derived molecule manufactured through recombinant DNA technology or hybridoma techniques. With respect to such biopharmaceutical products, "patented article" means an article embodying a patented invention relating to the composition of matter, process for producing, or use thereof; provided that such article is commercially exploited with the authorization of the patentee. The Central Government may, in consultation with the Controller, issue guidelines specifying criteria for determining whether a biopharmaceutical product qualifies as a “patented article” under this definition, particularly concerning processes incorporated within its manufacture and subsequent commercialization.

For the purposes of registration under these regulations, “patented article” shall be deemed to include any component part thereof, where such component’s manufacture is inextricably linked to the patented process. The Controller may require submission of detailed compositional analysis for articles claimed as a patented article, particularly if ambiguity exists regarding the scope of the patent itself. Any alteration or modification to a patented article which does not substantially affect its essential characteristics shall be considered permissible without requiring further registration, subject to verification by the Controller upon request from any interested party. The Registrar may issue directions concerning the marking of patented articles to ensure clarity and prevent misleading representations relating to the underlying patent.

Where an application for a patent is finally rejected, and such rejection arises solely from considerations relating to what are not inventions under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Appellate Board. The Board shall hear all parties interested in the matter and may allow the appeal if it finds that the invention does indeed constitute a novel and useful invention, or direct that the application be reconsidered by the Controller. Any order made by the Appellate Board shall be final subject only to further appeals as provided under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The applicant shall bear the burden of proving before the Appellate Board that the rejected matter falls outside the scope of what are not inventions and satisfies all other requirements for patentability.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, an invention shall be deemed to include any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or substantial improvement thereof. The Registrar may require submission of detailed schematics, flowcharts, and source code pertaining to computer-implemented inventions, alongside a formal declaration affirming originality and non-infringement of existing copyright. Any applicant seeking registration shall provide evidence demonstrating the novelty of the invention relative to prior art publications and previously registered patents. Furthermore, an application for registration may be rejected if it is determined that the claimed invention lacks sufficient inventive step or is otherwise excluded from patentability under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, an invention shall be deemed not to include discoveries of scientific principles or the formulation of a theory. An invention also excludes methods for agricultural or horticultural practice. Furthermore, inventions relating to literary, artistic or dramatic works are excluded from consideration. Any process for producing substances that is applied only in relation to substantially repeating matter will likewise not qualify as an invention. The Controller may require further documentation demonstrating novelty and non-obviousness if the application relates to a method of treatment of human beings. Entries on the register shall be considered conclusive evidence of such inventions, subject to any appeal under this Act.

An application for a certificate shall be deemed complete when it is accompanied by all required documentation, including detailed phenotypic data conforming to the guidelines issued by the Authority and evidence demonstrating distinctness. The Examining Officer may request further information from the applicant if clarity regarding any aspect of the plant variety or its characteristics is lacking. Upon receipt of a complete application, an acknowledgement shall be dispatched within thirty days. Publication of particulars relating to the application in the prescribed manner shall follow, allowing for objections by interested parties within sixty days thereafter. The Authority may grant or refuse the certificate based on the examination and any relevant objections received.

An applicant shall furnish, along with the application for a certificate of registration, detailed documentation demonstrating genetic uniformity and essential characteristics conforming to the variety description. The Authority may require further testing at designated institutions if inconsistencies are detected within the submitted data. Upon successful completion of all stipulated tests and verification procedures, and subject to compliance with prescribed guidelines regarding denomination selection, the applicant shall be notified in writing prior to final assessment. A certificate of registration shall only be issued where the variety meets established criteria for novelty, distinctiveness, stability, and uniformity; failure to satisfy any one criterion will result in rejection of the application.

An applicant aggrieved by a decision refusing the issue of a certificate may, within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. The appellate authority shall give notice to the Registrar and afford him an opportunity of being heard. Where the Appellate Board allows an appeal against refusal, it shall direct the Authority to proceed with the examination of the application as if the appeal had not been made. Any person whose interests are adversely affected by a certificate granted may petition the Intellectual Property Tribunal within ninety days from the date such certificate is advertised. The prescribed manner for filing appeals and petitions shall be followed strictly.

An applicant seeking a certificate of registration shall furnish, along with the application, detailed particulars regarding the expression of the plant variety and its essential characteristics. The Authority may require further documentation substantiating these claims, including data from field trials conducted according to established protocols. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall publish a notice in the prescribed manner inviting objections from any person interested in the matter. Any objection received shall be communicated to the applicant for response within the stipulated timeframe. The Authority shall consider all submissions before determining whether to grant or refuse the certificate of registration; unauthorized use constituting infringement will render the offender liable to penalties as determined by the Board.

Contributions to the gene fund shall be made by any person conducting research affecting plant varieties, subject to an assessment determined by the Authority based on the scale and potential commercial benefit derived from such research. Provided that institutions established solely for agricultural research and funded primarily through government grants are exempt from this requirement. The Authority may prescribe guidelines regarding acceptable forms of contribution, which may include monetary payments or in-kind contributions relating to germplasm accessions. Any funds received into the gene fund shall be utilized exclusively for supporting activities related to plant variety conservation, farmer training programs concerning intellectual property rights, and providing financial assistance to farmers undertaking research on indigenous varieties, all subject to annual audit by a chartered accountant appointed by the Central Government.

For the purposes of this Act, “benefit sharing” with respect to any plant variety shall include contributions made towards the *gene fund*. The Authority may determine the amount and modalities of such benefit sharing based on factors including, but not limited to, the extent of farmer participation in research and development related to the variety, the proportion of commercial sales attributable to varieties derived from indigenous germplasm, and the level of public investment directed toward conservation efforts. Contributions shall be made by any person or entity deriving a commercial advantage from the exploitation of plant genetic resources, subject to guidelines issued by the Central Government. The *gene fund* shall be utilized exclusively for supporting research relating to crop improvement, particularly involving under-utilized species and traditional varieties.

The Authority shall, in determining benefit sharing arrangements pursuant to commercial use of plant varieties for which Farmers’ Rights have been recognized, consider contributions made towards the replenishment of the Gene Fund. Such consideration shall include, but not be limited to, instances where a variety's essential derivation is attributable to traditional farming practices or indigenous knowledge. The Authority may require documentation substantiating such contribution prior to benefit determination. Details regarding any allocation from the Gene Fund for research and development relating to crop improvement shall be published in the Official Gazette annually. Any entity receiving funds from the Gene Fund shall comply with reporting requirements as prescribed by the Registering Authority, subject to periodic audits.

The Authority shall, upon receiving notification from any Plant Variety Protection Office of a contracting country regarding benefit sharing arrangements for plant varieties developed through the use of germplasm sourced in India, assess whether such arrangements adequately compensate Indian farmers and breeders. Any shortfall determined by the Authority shall be rectified through contributions to the Gene Fund. Contributions may be prescribed by regulations framed by the Central Government, taking into account factors including the extent of germplasm utilized, commercial value realized from the variety, and any existing agreements between the applicant and Indian institutions. The Authority may require further information from applicants demonstrating compliance with these requirements prior to granting protection.

For the purposes of this Act, an extant variety shall be deemed to have been pre-existing if it has been cultivated and propagated in India for at least three generations prior to the date of application for registration. The Authority may require the applicant to furnish documentary evidence substantiating the existence and cultivation history of the claimed extant variety, including records of farmers’ fields, seed exchanges, or other relevant documentation demonstrating its presence within Indian agricultural practices. Provided that, if the applicant demonstrates through scientific data a clear absence of prior record pertaining to the specific combination of traits exhibited by the variety, the Authority may waive this evidentiary requirement subject to further scrutiny and expert assessment.

For the purposes of this Act, an extant variety shall be deemed to have been pre-existing if it has been cultivated and propagated in India for at least three generations prior to the date of application for registration. The Authority may require the applicant to furnish documentary evidence demonstrating such cultivation and propagation, including records of seed distribution or farm practices. Provided that, where the applicant can demonstrate through oral testimony from farmers or other relevant stakeholders a history of cultivation predating three generations but lacking formal documentation, the Authority shall consider this as supplementary evidence. An extant variety may still be registrable if it possesses novel characteristics not previously observed in any registered variety and meets all other requirements for registration under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, an extant variety shall be deemed to possess distinctiveness only if it exhibits stable inheritance of its expression and remains uniform in reproduction or propagation. The Authority may require submission of data pertaining to morphological characteristics, genetic purity, and yield stability for assessment against established benchmarks. Provided that, where a farmer has cultivated a variety demonstrating traits consistent with an extant variety over at least three successive generations, the applicant shall furnish evidence substantiating such cultivation practices and their impact on varietal expression. Further, any licence granted in respect of a registered variety incorporating elements derived from an extant variety must specify royalty rates reflecting the contribution of that pre-existing genetic material.

For the purposes of this Act, an extant variety shall be deemed to have been pre-existing if it has a record of its existence for at least seven years immediately prior to the date of application. The Central Government may require evidence substantiating such pre-existence, including but not limited to farmers’ knowledge, traditional practices, and documentation from agricultural institutions. An applicant seeking registration shall provide details regarding the geographical location where the extant variety has been cultivated and utilized. Provided that if an extant variety is found to possess unique traits or characteristics demonstrably different from previously documented varieties, the Central Government may conduct further investigation before determining its eligibility for registration as a novel variety.

The Copyright Board shall have power to entertain appeals against orders passed by the Registrar under this Act relating to rectification of entries in the Register of Copyrights. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar may appeal to the Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order. The Board may, after giving notice to all concerned and affording them a reasonable opportunity for being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse such order. Costs relating to any appeal shall be determined by the Board in its discretion. The Central Government may make rules prescribing the procedure for appeals before the Copyright Board, subject to principles of natural justice. It is provided that the Board’s decision shall be final and binding, save for an appeal to a High Court on a point of law.

The Copyright Board shall have power to entertain appeals against orders passed by the Registrar under this Act relating to rectification of entries in the Register of Copyrights. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar may appeal to the Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order. The Board may, after giving notice to all concerned and affording them a reasonable opportunity for being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse such order. Decisions made by the Board are final subject to further appeals only on grounds specified in this Act concerning substantial questions of law. The Central Government may make rules prescribing the procedure for proceedings before the Copyright Board, provided that these rules shall not abridge any right conferred under this Act.

The Copyright Board shall, in consultation with the Registrar, formulate regulations pertaining to the registration of literary works adapted from folklore. These regulations may prescribe specific procedures for establishing authorship where traditional knowledge is incorporated into a derivative work. The Central Government has power to make rules regarding the submission of documentation demonstrating due acknowledgement and attribution to the originating community or source. Such rules shall detail requirements concerning linguistic translation, cultural sensitivity assessments, and verification processes undertaken by recognized folklore institutions. Further, the Registrar may issue guidelines for applicants seeking registration under this provision, clarifying acceptable formats and evidentiary standards.

The Copyright Board shall have power to entertain petitions seeking redressal against actions taken by copyright owners restricting access to works in digital form. Such actions include, but are not limited to, technological protection measures employed to prevent circumvention or unauthorized use. The Board may order a copyright owner to grant a non-exclusive licence for specific uses of the work if it determines that the restriction unreasonably prejudices public interest or impedes research and educational activities. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Copyright Board may appeal to the relevant High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. The Central Government shall make rules prescribing procedures for hearings before the Board, including timelines for disposal of petitions.

Where, upon revocation of a *patent granted*, any person aggrieved by the decision of the Controller may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order revoking the patent and shall state specifically the grounds on which the appellant considers the decision to be erroneous in law or fact. The Board may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to all parties concerned, confirm, vary, or reverse the decision appealed against. Costs relating to such appeal shall be determined by the Appellate Board according to principles of equity. Any party dissatisfied with the order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of that order.

For the purposes of this Act, a *patent granted* shall be deemed invalid if it is established to the satisfaction of the Controller that the invention was not novel at the date of filing of the application for the patent. Such determination may be made upon review of prior publications or public knowledge existing before said date, irrespective of whether such information was disclosed in India. The burden of proving lack of novelty shall rest with the party alleging invalidity. Provided that, if the applicant demonstrates diligent inquiry into relevant databases and publicly accessible records preceding the filing date, the Controller may consider this a mitigating factor when assessing the validity claim. Any challenge to the patent’s validity must be brought within six months from the grant of the patent.

Where any party aggrieved by a *patent granted* considers that the grant thereof is invalid, such party may file an opposition within six months from the date on which the application for the patent was published in the Official Gazette. The Controller shall afford all parties an opportunity of being heard, both sides being allowed to adduce evidence. If the opposition is successful, the *patent granted* shall be deemed to have never been valid and any acts done or goods made in contravention of the revoked patent may be subject to remedies available under this Act. The Controller may order compensation to be paid by the applicant for the patent to the opponent if it is shown that the applicant acted unreasonably in pursuing the application.

Where any interested person considers that a *patent granted* is obtained contrary to this Act, or that the invention claimed is not novel or obvious under the law, such person may file an opposition within six months from the date of publication of the grant. The Controller shall give notice of the opposition to the patentee and provide him with a reasonable opportunity to present his case and evidence in rebuttal. If, after considering all materials presented, the Controller finds that the grounds for opposition are well-founded, he may revoke the *patent granted* entirely or amend the claims to restrict the scope of protection. The right to oppose shall be forfeited if the interested person has failed to pursue diligent *registration* proceedings relating to the same invention within a period of three years from the date of first application.

The Authority shall prescribe a schedule of fees payable for various services rendered under this Act, including but not limited to applications for registration of plant varieties, maintenance of records pertaining to farmers’ rights, and conducting tests as per established protocols. Provided that an application made by a farmer claiming recognition of their contribution in the evolution of a variety shall be subject to reduced fees, commensurate with their economic status, as determined by the relevant District Authority. Any fee once paid is non-refundable except where an application is rejected on grounds unrelated to the applicant’s compliance with prescribed procedures or submission of inaccurate information. The Authority may revise the schedule periodically, giving at least three months' notice through public notification.

The Authority may, upon receipt of a complete application for registration of a plant variety, require submission of additional documentation pertaining to the applicant’s financial solvency. Such documentation must demonstrate consistent adherence to payment schedules established by the Authority. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence of ongoing compliance with these requirements shall result in suspension of processing until all outstanding obligations are fulfilled. The prescribed fees for initial examination and subsequent grant of protection shall be remitted electronically, subject to any exemptions granted under existing regulations concerning smallholder farmers. Any applicant failing to remit the requisite fees within ninety days from the date of demand notice will have their application deemed withdrawn, without further notification.

Where an application for registration is rejected due to non-payment of prescribed fees, the applicant may, within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of rejection, submit a fresh application accompanied by the requisite fees and any applicable late payment surcharges. Such resubmission shall be treated as a new application under this Act and subject to all procedural requirements for initial filing. Failure to remit the outstanding fees within the stipulated period will preclude further consideration of the original or subsequent applications relating to the same plant variety. The Authority may, in its discretion, waive late payment surcharges where it is satisfied that the failure to pay was due to circumstances beyond the applicant’s reasonable control.

The Authority may, through notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe the amount of fees payable for applications for registration of plant varieties. Such fees shall be differentiated based on the category of applicant – namely, public sector institutions, small and marginal farmers, tribal groups, and commercial entities – with preferential rates applicable to the former three categories. The Authority may review these prescribed fees periodically, not less than once every five years, considering prevailing economic conditions and the administrative costs incurred in processing applications. Any revision shall be published for public comment prior to implementation. All fees remitted are subject to adjustments as determined by the Central Government from time to time.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered design shall submit an application in the prescribed form to the Designs Office, detailing the particulars of the alleged error or omission. Such application must be supported by evidence demonstrating that the registration infringes upon existing prior rights or is otherwise contrary to established principles of design law. The Designs Office may require further documentation from the applicant substantiating these claims and shall provide a reasonable opportunity for any registered proprietor whose interests are affected to file a counter-statement. Rectification will only be ordered if, following due consideration of all submissions, it is determined that the continued validity of the registered designs would constitute an inequity or prejudice public interest.

An application for registration of a registered design shall include particulars specifying the article to which the design is applied or intended to be applied, together with details regarding any colour or material used therein. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish additional information deemed necessary for proper examination and assessment of novelty. Where an applicant has previously filed an identical design relating to the same article, the application shall be rejected without further consideration. Any person aggrieved by a refusal of registration may appeal to the Controller within three months from the date of communication of such refusal. The Registrar shall maintain a register of registered designs accessible for public inspection upon payment of the prescribed fee.

An application for registration of a registered design shall be refused if the design is not new or does not involve an aesthetic feature. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars concerning the process by which the design was arrived at, and such information as he deems necessary to ascertain compliance with these provisions. Where a registered design incorporates elements derived from prior published works, the application shall include a detailed explanation demonstrating originality sufficient for registration. Any person aggrieved by a refusal of registration may appeal to the Controller within sixty days of receipt of notification of the decision. The register maintained under this Act is open for public inspection during normal business hours, subject to any restrictions imposed by the Registrar to protect confidential information relating to registered designs.

For the purposes of this Act, "broadcast reproduction right" with respect to any broadcast includes the exclusive right to make copies of the programme in its entirety or substantial portions thereof and offer such copies for sale or hire, or distribute them in any other manner. This right shall accrue to the owner of copyright in the work comprising the programme, subject to any terms specified in a contractual assignment of rights relating to the broadcast. The making of a copy under this provision is deemed a reproduction within the meaning of this Act. Provided that, where a broadcaster obtains a license to communicate a work to the public, the exercise of the broadcast reproduction right shall not extend beyond the scope of such licensed communication.

For the purposes of this Act, an application for registration as a broadcaster shall include particulars relating to each programme broadcast by the applicant and from which a *broadcast reproduction right* may arise. Such particulars shall specify the date and time of the original transmission, the geographical area covered by the broadcast, and details regarding any subsequent distribution or adaptation of the broadcast signal. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the claim of ownership of the copyright in respect of works incorporated within a broadcast programme. Where a broadcaster licenses copyrighted material for inclusion in a broadcast, the terms of that license shall be deemed relevant when assessing the scope of permissible acts relating to the *broadcast reproduction right*.

For the purposes of this Act, a broadcast reproduction right shall subsist in respect of every telecast and videocast signal comprising works protected by copyright. Such right shall extend to include the making of copies from any such signal, provided that the copying is undertaken within thirty days following the initial broadcast. Any person intending to make such copies for commercial purposes must first apply to the Registrar, submitting details including the nature of the work reproduced and the intended quantity of reproductions. The Registrar may require further information to ascertain compliance with conditions relating to equitable remuneration payable to right owners. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements shall render any subsequent reproduction infringing under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "broadcast reproduction right" shall mean the exclusive right to make copies of a broadcast signal for subsequent rebroadcast or other use, subject to reasonable alteration to ensure contemporaneity. This right extends only to signals transmitted by broadcasting stations duly registered with the appropriate licensing authority and includes the right to store such copies in any medium, whether digital or analogue. The making of a copy without authorization shall be deemed an infringement. Any person claiming entitlement to this broadcast reproduction right may apply for registration of their claim before the Copyright Board; provided that such registration is merely prima facie evidence of ownership and does not confer exclusive rights beyond those established under this Act.

The Controller shall, upon receiving an application for registration of a patent relating to a process involving a novel chemical compound, and being satisfied that such process is essential for national security, issue secrecy directions. Such directions shall specify the duration for which disclosure of details pertaining to the manufacturing method may be withheld from public access. The applicant shall furnish two copies of the specification, marked “Confidential – Subject to Secrecy Directions,” to the Controller. These documents are not open to inspection by any person other than authorized officials and those specifically permitted under written authorization from the Controller. Secrecy directions to be periodically reviewed every three years, with opportunity for objection afforded to the applicant.

Where the Controller considers an application for patent involves a process or technology deemed critical national infrastructure, they shall issue secrecy directions. Such directions prohibit disclosure of details pertaining to the claimed invention until specified conditions are met. These conditions include certification by the designated authority that public dissemination would compromise national security or essential services. Failure to comply with a secrecy direction constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment and fine. The Controller may, at intervals not exceeding three years, review any existing secrecy directions and shall provide affected applicants written notice of such reviews, affording them opportunity for representation before modification or revocation is considered.

The Controller shall, upon receiving an application for a patent relating to a process or substance which is deemed critical infrastructure technology, consider whether a secrecy direction is warranted. Such determination shall be based on representations submitted by the applicant and any counter-representations filed by interested parties. The applicant may propose terms of a non-exclusive licence granting rights to utilize the invention subject to conditions stipulated within the secrecy direction. Any such licence must specify the duration for which the confidentiality obligations remain in force, not exceeding ten years from the date of grant of the patent. The Controller shall periodically review any existing secrecy directions relating to critical infrastructure technology, at intervals not less than five years, and may modify or revoke them based on updated assessments of national security concerns.

The Controller shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a patent relating to a process involving genetically modified organisms and deemed by the Central Government to possess strategic implications, issue secrecy directions. Such directions shall prescribe the manner in which documentation pertaining to the invention’s development, including but not limited to experimental data and manufacturing protocols, is stored and accessed. The applicant shall furnish an undertaking confirming adherence to these prescribed measures. Failure to comply with a secrecy direction may result in suspension of patent examination proceedings. These secrecy directions are subject to periodic review by a committee constituted for that purpose, ensuring continued relevance and efficacy without unduly hindering innovation.

Where a plant variety is registered and commercialized utilizing genetic material obtained directly from farmers’ fields without prior authorization, the Authority may direct the registrant to provide monetary compensation to those affected farmers. Such compensation shall be determined based on the extent of contribution made by the farmer's germplasm towards the development of the registered variety, as assessed through established scientific protocols. The determination of benefit sharing is subject to a right of appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of notification of the Authority’s order. Failure to comply with an order regarding benefit sharing may result in revocation of registration and imposition of penalties not exceeding five times the annual gross royalty income derived from the infringing variety.

For the purposes of this Act, “benefit sharing” with respect to any registered plant variety shall be determined by the Authority based on a written agreement between the breeder and any person utilizing propagating material derived from that variety. Such agreements must specify the percentage share allocated to farmers who have contributed significantly towards the enhancement of traits in the initial breeding process, subject to guidelines issued by the Central Government. The Authority may require demonstration, through documented field trials or other verifiable means, establishing such farmer contribution prior to recognizing a claim for benefit sharing. Any dispute regarding the interpretation or implementation of these agreements shall be referred to an arbitration panel appointed by the Authority.

For the purposes of this Act, “benefit sharing” with respect to a registered plant variety shall be determined based on the terms and conditions stipulated in the application for registration. An applicant seeking registration may propose a scheme outlining the distribution of benefits arising from commercialization, including but not limited to licensing fees, royalties, and sales proceeds derived from the protected variety. The Authority shall review such proposed schemes during examination of the application and may require modifications to ensure equitable consideration is given to contributions made by farmers or rural communities in the initial discovery or development process. Failure to adequately address benefit sharing considerations may result in refusal of registration, subject to appeal before an Appellate Board.

Where a plant variety has been developed using germplasm obtained from indigenous sources, and where that development involved contributions by farmers, rural communities, or traditional agricultural practices, the Authority may direct the breeder to provide for benefit sharing. Such direction shall specify the proportion of benefits accruing to the breeder which are to be shared, and the manner in which such sharing is implemented. The details of any directed benefit-sharing arrangement shall be published in the Official Gazette. Failure by a breeder to comply with an order issued under this provision renders them liable for penalties as determined by the Authority, subject to appeal before the Appellate Board.

Where a patent application is found to contain information not in the public domain prior to the filing date, and it is determined that this non-disclosure resulted from an act or omission attributable to a *director* of the applicant company, the Controller may issue a notice requiring the company to demonstrate due diligence in preventing such disclosure. The notice shall specify the grounds for concern and provide a period not exceeding sixty days within which the company must submit its response. Failure by the company to adequately address the concerns raised in the notice, or submission of demonstrably false information, will render the application liable for rejection. Any officer authorized by the Controller may conduct inspections relevant to verifying compliance with this procedure.

Where a patent application is found to contain information not in accordance with prescribed standards regarding prior art disclosures, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish an affidavit affirming compliance with regulations pertaining to inventive step. If the applicant fails to provide such an affidavit within thirty days of notification, or if the affidavit contains materially false statements, the Controller shall issue a notice to the company’s director responsible for patent prosecution. The director shall then have fifteen days to submit evidence demonstrating due diligence in ensuring adherence to disclosure protocols. Failure to comply with this directive may result in suspension of the applicant's privileges regarding future filings and potential referral to appropriate disciplinary authorities.

Where a patent has been granted under this Act, and it is established that an act infringing upon the rights conveyed by the patent was committed with the knowledge or consent of a director of the company holding the patent, such director shall be jointly and severally liable with the company for damages sustained by the claimant. The Controller may, subject to due process, issue a licence permitting use of the patented invention if it is demonstrated that the infringement arose from instructions issued directly by said director acting outside the scope of their authority as defined in the company’s articles of incorporation. Any appeal against such licensing decision shall be heard expeditiously and with consideration for the potential impact on ongoing commercial operations.

Where a patent application is found to contain information not prescribed by the Regulations under this Act, or where representations made within an application are demonstrably false, the Controller may issue a notice requiring clarification from the applicant. Such notice shall specify the deficiencies identified and provide a period of ninety days for response. If, following such response, the Controller remains satisfied that the patentee’s actions constitute wilful misrepresentation, liability shall extend to every director of the company at the time of filing, unless it is demonstrated that they were unaware of, and did not consent to, the misleading information. The Controller may, in addition to any other penalties prescribed, direct the applicant to pay costs incurred by the Office in investigating the matter.

An application for registration may be subject to review by the Controller if a representation is received alleging that the layout design was, at the time of filing the application, not original. Such representation shall detail the grounds upon which originality is challenged and provide supporting documentation demonstrating prior publication or disclosure inconsistent with novelty. The Controller shall serve notice on the applicant, affording them an opportunity to submit a written response addressing the allegations. Following consideration of both the representation and the applicant’s reply, the Controller may direct that the registration be cancelled if satisfied that the layout design lacks originality as defined under this Act. Any order for cancelling registration shall specify the reasons thereof.

An application for registration may be subject to a proceeding for *cancelling registration* if it is demonstrated that the layout design was, at the time of its first commercial exploitation anywhere in the world, not an original work. For the purposes of this provision, "original" signifies that the layout design reflects the author's own intellectual effort and skill, and does not directly or substantially derive from any prior published layout designs. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, constitute tribunals to hear and determine appeals arising from orders passed under this Act relating to such proceedings. Any party aggrieved by an order of a tribunal may further appeal to the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the registered office of the applicant for registration is situated.

An application for cancellation of registration may be made to the Registrar by any person aggrieved by an entry in the register. Such application shall state specifically the grounds upon which it is based and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the relevant portion of the register. The Registrar, after giving notice to the registered layout-design owner and affording them an opportunity of being heard, may direct that the registration be cancelled if he considers that any ground for cancellation exists under this Act. Any party aggrieved by such direction may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all applications received and orders passed relating to cancelling registration.

An application for registration may be subject to review if it is brought to the attention of the Registrar that the layout design incorporates elements substantially derived from a previously registered layout design, or an unregistered layout design which has been disclosed. The Registrar shall provide notice to the applicant detailing the alleged infringement and specifying the relevant prior design. The applicant shall then have sixty days to submit a written response demonstrating compliance with provisions regarding originality of design. Failure by the applicant to adequately address these concerns within the stipulated timeframe, or demonstrable evidence that the layout design was copied without authorization, will empower the Registrar to initiate proceedings for cancelling registration.

For the purposes of this Act, a “registered design” means original designs where applied in a three-dimensional form to articles of manufacture. An article of manufacture shall include any work or composition which, by being made or assembled, is given a definite shape and character. A design is deemed registered upon its entry into the Register of Designs. The Controller may require an applicant for registration to amend the drawings or other particulars relating to the design before finally accepting it for registration; provided that such amendment does not alter the identity of the design as claimed in the application. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller regarding acceptance or rejection of a registered design shall have recourse to appeal, subject to prescribed procedures and fees.

An applicant aggrieved by a refusal to register a design or by the revocation of registration thereof may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within three months from the date of receipt of the order appealed against. The Board shall give notice to the Controller and opportunity to be heard, and may confirm, vary, or reverse the decision appealed from. Where an application for registration contains more than one design, the Registrar may require the applicant to elect which of such designs he intends to register as a single registered design, provided that each selected design is separately capable of serving the purpose for which a design is registered. The Controller shall publish particulars of any registered design in the Designs Journal.

Subject to compliance with sub-paragraph (1), a proprietor of a registered design shall be entitled to grant a licence conferring rights relating to the manufacture, use, or sale of an article embodying the design. Such licence agreement must specify the duration and geographical extent of the granted rights, and any royalties payable by the licensee. The Controller may require submission of the proposed licence terms for review prior to registration if concerns arise regarding potential anti-competitive practices. Any government department seeking to exploit a registered design shall first obtain written consent from the proprietor, provided that such consent may be subject to conditions relating to fair compensation and non-prejudice to public interest considerations.

For the purposes of this Act, a “registered design” means a proprietary right granted in respect of the visual appearance of an article or part thereof, arising from its shape, configuration, pattern, ornament or composition of lines or colours applied to it. An application for registration of a design shall disclose sufficient detail to enable a person skilled in the trade to reproduce the design and shall include representations such as drawings or photographs clearly depicting the design claimed. The Controller may require further particulars relating to an application if deemed necessary for proper examination. A registered design confers upon the proprietor the exclusive right to apply the design, or any substantially similar design, to articles offered for sale or used by them.

For the purposes of this Act, an “international application” shall mean an application filed with a receiving Office designated by contracting states under the Patent Cooperation Treaty. Such international applications shall be treated in relation to examination and grant as if they were domestic applications filed on the date specified therein, subject to any modifications or clarifications deemed necessary by the Controller. The applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence relating to the filing of the international application as may be prescribed. Where an international application claims priority from an earlier application, particulars of that earlier application shall be included in the accompanying form and verified accordingly. Any fees paid in respect of the international application may, subject to regulations framed by the Central Government, be credited towards payment of official fees under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, an “international application” includes any application filed with a Receiving Office designated under the Patent Cooperation Treaty and subsequently proceeding to designation of India. The Controller General shall establish procedures for facilitating communication between the Indian patent office and the International Bureau concerning such applications, including but not limited to the transmission of copies of requests, declarations, and other documents required by the Patent Cooperation Treaty. Any fees payable in respect of an international application shall be determined according to regulations framed by the Central Government, subject to any adjustments necessary to reflect variations in exchange rates as notified from time to time. The particulars of such designated Receiving Offices will be published periodically in the Official Gazette.

For the purposes of this Act, “receiving office” shall mean any office designated by the Controller under notification in the Official Gazette to receive applications and documents relating to international applications filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty. An “international application”, with respect to this Act, includes an application made pursuant to the Patent Cooperation Treaty wherein India is nominated as a designated State; such application shall be treated as if it were an application for grant of patent in India from the date specified therein. The Controller may prescribe forms and procedures for processing international applications received at receiving offices, subject to the provisions of the Patent Cooperation Treaty and any regulations framed thereunder. Any communication relating to an international application shall be addressed through the designated receiving office.

For the purposes of this Act, “international application” includes any application filed with a designated receiving office under the Patent Cooperation Treaty. An applicant intending to seek protection for an invention in India and who has previously filed an international application designating India shall be required to furnish along with the patent application a certified copy of the aforementioned international application, including the description, claims, and drawings as originally filed. The Controller may require such further particulars relating to the registration of the international application as he deems necessary for examination purposes. Failure to provide this documentation shall render the application liable to rejection, subject to the applicant’s right to amend or otherwise satisfy the requirements at a later stage during processing.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,—(a) "Appellate Board" means an authority constituted for hearing and determining appeals from orders passed by the Registrar under this Act relating to copyright disputes; (b) "copyright" includes the exclusive right to authorize others to reproduce the work in any material form, to issue copies of the work to the public, to perform the work in public, to communicate the work to the public by wireless signs or other means, and to translate the work into a different language. Subject to the provisions contained herein, certain disputes relating to copyright may be decided by the Appellate Board as provided under this Act.

2-5-1978, vide notification No. S.O. 666, dated 15-2-1978, in respect of the provisions of

patentee means a person to whom a patent has been granted under this Act and includes any person who is entitled to be such a patentee by virtue of an assignment or other transfer of rights conferred by the patent. A patentee may, subject to the conditions prescribed herein, grant licences in respect of his invention to one or more persons, provided that no licence shall prejudice the exclusive right vested in him under this Act. The grant of a licence does not affect the copyright subsisting in any literary, dramatic, musical, and artistic works related to the patented invention unless such copyright is specifically assigned by the patentee.

No assignment of a trade mark shall be valid unless it is in writing signed by the assignor or his duly authorised agent. Such an assignment must identify the trade mark, specify the rights assigned, including but not limited to exclusive use, licensing, or co-existence with other marks, and detail the duration and territorial extent of such assignment. The assignment may also stipulate any conditions precedent or subsequent for the validity of the same. Provided that the Registrar of Trade Marks shall have the power to reject an assignment if it is found to be in contravention of this Act or any rules made thereunder.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,—(a) "breeder" means any person who is the developer and holder of rights in respect of a plant variety protected under this Act; (b) "application" refers to the formal request submitted by a breeder for protection of a new plant variety. Subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, an application shall contain all necessary information required for evaluation of the novelty, distinctiveness, uniformity and stability of the claimed variety. Any person who wishes to apply for protection under this Act shall submit the application in the form and manner specified by the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Authority (hereinafter referred to as "the Authority"). The Authority may require additional information or clarification from the applicant before processing the application, provided that such requirements do not unreasonably delay the process.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,—(a) "breeder" means any person who is the developer and holder of rights in respect of a plant variety protected under this Act; (b) "registration", in relation to a plant variety, means the formal recognition granted by the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Authority for the protection of such variety. Subject to the provisions contained herein, a breeder shall apply for registration within six months from the date of commercial exploitation of the variety or such other period as may be prescribed by the Authority. Provided that in case of any breach of this provision, the Authority may, on payment of a fee, grant retrospective registration upon satisfaction of certain conditions as may be specified by it.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,—(p) "registered proprietor" includes any person who is entitled under the terms of registration as the owner of a trade mark and may include any legal personal representative of such person; (q) "Registrar" means the Registrar appointed for the time being to carry out the provisions of this Act. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Registrar shall have all powers necessary or expedient for the purpose of performing his functions under this Act, including the power to issue directions and make orders as may be required for the registration and maintenance of trade marks.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,—(a) "author" means and includes—(i) the person who creates an original work; (ii) where the making of an unpublished work is extended over a considerable period, the last surviving author at any time during which such work was being created or made. Provided that in determining whether the making of a work has been extended over a considerable period, regard shall be had to all relevant circumstances including but not limited to the nature and extent of the contribution by each individual involved in the creation or continuation of the work.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,—(a) "author" means the person who creates an original work and includes—(i) where the making of unpublished work is extended over a considerable period, all persons who have contributed to its creation; (b) "licence", in relation to copyright, means any agreement by which one or more rights conferred by this Act are granted, permitted, restricted, or prohibited for consideration. Subject to the provisions of this Act, an author may grant a licence to another person to use his work. Provided that no such licence shall be valid unless it is in writing and signed by the author or with the authority of the author.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,—(a) "sound recording" means any work containing sounds fixed on any medium and capable of being heard when played back by mechanical or electronic device; (b) where a sound recording is used in connection with a trade mark for promoting goods or services, such use shall be deemed to infringe the copyright in the sound recording unless the owner of the sound recording has given consent. Subject to any agreement between the parties, the owner of a sound recording may bring an action against any person who without his consent uses the sound recording in connection with a trade mark for promoting goods or services, provided that such use is likely to cause confusion among consumers regarding the origin of the goods or services.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires—(l) "performer" means an individual who delivers a performance and includes any person who makes arrangements for the delivery of such a performance; provided that nothing in this sub-clause shall prejudice the rights of the copyright owner under other provisions of this Act. Performers are entitled to protection against unauthorized use, broadcasting, or communication to the public of their performances without their consent. Any commercial exploitation of a performer's work by another person without due authorization is liable to be treated as an infringement and may result in civil remedies including injunctions, damages, and accounts of profits.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires—(l) "performer" includes an individual who performs a literary, dramatic, musical, or any other artistic work by recitation, acting, singing, dancing, or in any other manner; and (m) "performance" means any act of doing anything by way of representation before any audience whether live or broadcasted. Subject to the provisions contained herein, a performer shall have the exclusive right to authorize or prohibit the broadcasting, communication to the public, rental, lending, or making available of his performance in relation to a fixation of such performance, and no person other than the performer may exercise such rights without his consent.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires—(l) "performer" means an individual who performs a literary, artistic, or scientific work by recitation, rendering, acting, dancing, singing, or any other means; and (m) "prescribed" refers to such matters as may be specified in rules made under this Act. Subject to the provisions of this Act, a performer shall have the exclusive right to authorize or prohibit the broadcasting of his performance in public, including by wireless signs, signals, sounds, or images, either directly or through any device or process, and also the fixation of such performance on any medium from which it can be reproduced. This right may not be exercised in contravention of any agreement entered into between a performer and another party unless such agreement is in writing and signed by the performer.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires—(l) "performer" includes an individual who performs a literary, dramatic, musical, or any other intellectual performance and also includes a body corporate performing such a work; (m) "design" means a new design having a special aesthetic appeal and capable of being applied to industrial products. Subject to the provisions contained in this Act, a performer shall have the exclusive right to authorize or prohibit the broadcasting of his performance by any means of wireless telecommunications, including the fixation thereof on any medium from which it can be replayed. This right shall subsist for a period of twenty years from the date of the first broadcast of such performance. Provided that nothing in this subsection shall prevent the performer from authorizing or prohibiting the use of his performance for the purpose of teaching or research, subject to payment of reasonable remuneration as may be determined by an appropriate authority.

For the purposes of this Act, a record called the Register of Trade Marks shall be kept at the head office of the Trade Marks Registry wherein all registered trade marks with their respective classes, proprietor's name, address, description, and any notifications of assignment or transmission shall be entered. The register may also contain particulars of registered users, conditions, limitations, and such other information as may be prescribed by rules made under this Act. Any alteration in the details recorded in the Register of Trade Marks shall be effected only after due verification and approval by the Registrar of Trade Marks.

(farmer) "farmer" includes an individual, a group of individuals, a legal entity, and any institution engaged in traditional farming practices or modern agriculture for subsistence purposes or small-scale commercial production but not including large-scale commercial farmers. A farmer shall be entitled to apply for registration of his variety if he has developed the variety through traditional knowledge or methods without any external genetic material. Subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, a farmer's right in respect of registered varieties shall include the right to receive a fair share of benefits arising from the use of such varieties by others.

A patent agent shall be a person who has been registered under this Act and whose name appears on the register maintained by the Controller for such purposes. A patent agent may act as an attorney or representative before any authority constituted under this Act, including the Patent Office and the Opposition Board, with respect to matters related to patents. Subject to the provisions of this Act, a patent agent shall be entitled to practice in all respects as if he were an advocate within the meaning of any law for the time being in force relating to advocates. However, no person other than a registered patent agent may act or purport to act as such before any authority constituted under this Act without the express permission of the Controller.

A patent agent shall be a person who has been registered under this Act. The registration of a patent agent may be granted subject to such conditions as the Controller may prescribe, including passing an examination and furnishing security for compliance with the provisions of this Act. A patent agent so registered shall have all rights and privileges conferred by or under this Act in relation to his practice as a patent agent, provided that he acts within the limits of his registration. Any person who practices as a patent agent without being duly registered as such shall be liable to such penalties as may be prescribed.

For the purposes of this Act, "infringing copy" shall mean and include any copy of a work that is made without the consent of the owner of the copyright in such work, where such making of the copy results in an infringement of the exclusive rights conferred by this Act. Such infringement may occur when the copy is used for the purpose of trade or commerce, or communicated to the public, distributed, sold, let for hire, or otherwise disposed of to the public by way of business, without the authorization of the owner of the copyright. Subject to any other provisions of this Act, an infringing copy shall be deemed to have been made and used in contravention of the exclusive rights conferred upon the owner of the copyright.

For the purposes hereof, "infringing copy" shall mean and include any copy of an Indian work that is reproduced without the permission of the owner of copyright in such work, where such reproduction is made by way of—(a) making a substantial part of the work available to the public; (b) preparing a translation or adaptation of the work; or (c) using the work for any commercial purpose. Subject to the provisions of this Act, no person shall make, import, sell, distribute, hire out, exhibit in public, communicate to the public by wire or wireless means, or otherwise deal with an infringing copy without the authority of the owner of copyright in such Indian work. Provided that nothing herein contained shall prevent any person from dealing with a copy of an Indian work if such dealing is for private and domestic use only.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires—(a) "infringing copy" means a copy of a work made without the consent of the owner of the copyright in such work and which copies the whole or a substantial part of the work; (b) "application" means an application for registration of a design filed under this Act. Subject to the provisions contained herein, any person who makes, imports, sells, distributes, rents, hires out, exhibits publicly, communicates to the public by wire or wireless means, or otherwise deals with in any manner infringing copies of a work shall be deemed to have infringed the copyright in such work and may be liable for civil remedies as provided under this Act. Provided that nothing herein contained shall affect the validity of an application filed prior to the date on which it is declared that making, selling, or distributing infringing copies has commenced.

patent office shall maintain and keep up to date records of all patents, applications for patents, and other documents relevant thereto. Such records shall be open for inspection by any person during normal working hours subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. The patent office may, at its discretion, provide copies of the records upon payment of fees as may be determined from time to time. Any discrepancy or error in the records maintained by the patent office shall be rectified on receipt of a verified application made within six months from the date of discovery of such discrepancy or error.

registration shall be made by the applicant in writing and signed by him, stating his name and address, the title or brief description of the invention for which he seeks registration, and such other particulars as may be prescribed. the application for registration shall also contain a specification describing the invention fully and in clear terms and manner, disclosing the best mode known to the inventor of carrying out the invention, together with drawings if necessary. upon receipt of the application, the patent office shall examine it to ensure compliance with all statutory requirements before proceeding further with the registration process.

(a) "copyright owner" means the person who has the exclusive right to authorize or prohibit the use of any work under copyright law, and includes any legal successor in title.

(b) The term "patent office" refers to the authority responsible for receiving, examining, and granting patents, as well as maintaining records related thereto. Any communication with respect to a patent application shall be addressed to the patent office or its authorized representative.

(c) Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming to be aggrieved by an action taken by the patent office may file a complaint within six months from the date of such action. The patent office shall provide a remedy in accordance with the principles of natural justice and the provisions of relevant laws.

A company, for the purposes of this Act, includes a body corporate formed under the laws of India and every local authority. Subject to the provisions herein contained, no patent shall be granted in respect of an invention made by or on behalf of a company unless such company has taken all reasonable steps to exploit the invention commercially within India or has assigned the right to apply for a patent to another person who undertakes to do so. Provided that nothing in this subsection shall prevent a company from assigning its rights under a contract entered into with any other party, provided such assignment is made in writing and registered as required by law.

Where an application for a patent is accompanied by a provisional specification, such provisional specification may contain a brief description of the invention, including its nature and utility, together with drawings or diagrams where necessary. The provisional specification shall clearly disclose the invention in sufficient detail to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same. Notwithstanding anything contained herein, a complete specification containing full particulars of the invention must be filed within twelve months from the date of filing of the application for patent. Failure to file such complete specification within the prescribed period shall result in the deemed abandonment of the application.

Where an application for a patent (not being a convention application or an application filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty designating India) is accompanied by a provisional specification, such provisional specification may contain only a brief description of the invention and its operation or use. The applicant shall file a complete specification within twelve months from the date of filing of the application; provided that where the applicant has filed a priority claim in respect of an earlier application, the period for filing the complete specification may be extended by six months. Failure to file a complete specification within the prescribed time limit shall result in the application being deemed abandoned.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,—(zzz) "visual recording" means a recording consisting of a series of related images which are being shown by any device or process in such a manner as to give the impression of moving pictures and includes cinematograph films. Subject to the provisions contained herein, no person shall make, publish, sell, hire, import for commercial purposes, communicate to the public, or otherwise deal with a visual recording without the permission of the owner of the copyright therein. Provided that nothing in this subsection shall prevent fair dealing for the purpose of research or private study.

An international application shall mean and include any application made under this Act by a person who is not ordinarily resident or has no business establishment within India but seeks to register a mark in respect of goods or services intended to be supplied into, or used in commerce within, the territory of India. The Trade Marks Registry may deal with such an international application subject to compliance with all necessary formalities and payment of prescribed fees. Provided that the Trade Marks Registry shall not entertain any international application where the applicant fails to provide adequate information regarding the goods or services for which protection is sought, or where there are reasonable grounds to believe that the mark applied for is likely to cause confusion or be detrimental to public order or morality.

Where an international application is received by the Trade Marks Registry under this Act, it shall be deemed to have been made on the date of receipt and the Registrar shall forthwith examine such application in accordance with the provisions of this Act. Subject to any agreement between India and another country or territory, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish additional information within a period not exceeding three months from the date of receipt of the international application. If the required information is furnished within the prescribed time, the Registrar shall proceed to examine the application; otherwise, it may be rejected on grounds of non-compliance with statutory requirements.

For the purposes of this Act, "registered layout" shall mean any original semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design that has been registered under the provisions herein. A registered layout may be granted protection subject to compliance with all applicable conditions and formalities as prescribed by rules made under this Act. The registration process shall ensure that the design is novel, non-obvious, and industrially applicable. Any person claiming a right in respect of a registered layout must do so within the time limits specified by such rules. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the revocation or refusal of registration.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,— (bb) "exclusive licence" means an agreement in writing between the patentee and another person whereby the latter is entitled to exercise within India, for the term of such exclusive licence, the right granted by the patent subject to any conditions mentioned therein; provided that the grantor shall not himself or authorize any other person to exercise such rights during the subsistence of such exclusive licence. (cc) "infringement" means the act of a person who without the consent of the patentee or the holder of an exclusive licence, exercises within India any right conferred by the patent; provided that nothing in this sub-clause shall affect the validity of any prior use of the invention made in good faith.

Where a person who is not the proprietor of a design registers such design under this Act, and subsequently it comes to light that he was not entitled to do so, the Registrar may, upon being satisfied that there has been no fraudulent or malicious intent on the part of the registrant, issue an order directing the removal of the name of such person from the register in respect of such design. The proprietor of the design shall be entitled to apply for rectification of the register and the Registrar shall, subject to any directions given by a court, comply with such application if satisfied that it is just and proper so to do.

Where a trade mark has been used by an individual and such use does not constitute registration under this Act, that individual may transmit his rights in such unregistered trade mark to another person by means of assignment or otherwise. Such transmission shall be subject to the condition that the assignee undertakes to comply with all obligations arising out of this Act as if he were originally registered for the said trade mark. Provided that where an unregistered trade mark is transmitted, the original user may continue to use such trade mark provided there is no prejudice caused to the interests of the assignee or any third party who has acquired rights in relation thereto.

Where a registered proprietor of a trade mark has established that there is likelihood of infringement by another party in respect of goods or services identical or similar to those covered by the registered trade mark, the court may grant an ex parte injunction restraining such other party from using any sign likely to be mistaken for the registered trade mark until such time as notice of the application and a copy of the order have been served on such other party. Provided that the court shall not grant an ex parte injunction unless it is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that immediate irreparable injury will be caused by the use of the sign in question, or that such injury cannot adequately be remedied by any other form of relief.

A "patented article" shall include any product, substance, device, or composition of matter specified in the claims of a granted patent. The Central Government may, by notification, specify additional categories of patented articles subject to such conditions as it deems fit. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the owner of a patent for a patented article shall have the exclusive right to make, use, sell, offer for sale, import and export such patented article within India or any part thereof during the term of the patent. Provided that nothing in this subsection shall prevent the Central Government from authorizing the making, using, selling, offering for sale, importing, or exporting of a patented article where it is satisfied that the public interest so requires.

A certificate of registration shall be issued by the Authority upon satisfaction of all conditions prescribed under this Act. The certificate shall specify the particulars including, but not limited to, the name and address of the plant breeder, details of the variety for which registration is granted, the date of grant, and any other relevant information as may be necessary. Subject to any condition or restriction imposed by the Authority, the holder of a certificate of registration shall have exclusive rights over the registered variety during the term specified in the certificate. Provided that nothing herein contained shall prejudice the rights of farmers under this Act.
